articles.title_original: Annealed Gibbs Measures with Data-Driven Interaction Potentials on Hierarchical Structures
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2606.30064v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We construct annealed Gibbs measures on continuous interaction parameters and binary spins on Cayley trees of order $k\geq 1$, with coupling functions determined by an empirical loss. The interaction parameters and spins are distinct random variables: the former determine edge couplings, while the latter represent binary labels. The training data specify the coupling function and the joint Gibbs specification, rather than automatically selecting a unique Gibbs measure on interaction parameters.
  We derive necessary and sufficient compatibility conditions for the finite-volume joint densities. These conditions take the form of nonlinear integral equations for boundary laws and characterize the splitting annealed Gibbs measures constructed here. For $k=1$, the translation-invariant equations reduce to positive compact integral operators. Under the stated hypotheses, they have a unique normalized positive solution. For $k=2$, an explicit empirical-loss kernel reduces the translation-invariant equations to polynomial equations. In this case, we show that hierarchical learning systems may exhibit phase-transition phenomena: for certain empirical kernels on Cayley trees order two, multiple Gibbs measures on spins emerge beyond a critical inverse temperature, corresponding to distinct equilibrium prediction regimes.
  For a selected annealed Gibbs measure, we distinguish its marginal on interaction parameters from its conditional Gibbs measures on spins at fixed interaction parameters.
  Our results provide a new perspective on energy-based learning, where data do not merely determine an optimal model through minimization but define an entire probabilistic landscape of possible inference states.

articles.title_original: Localized LoRA-MoE: Mixture of Low-Rank Experts With Adaptive Routing
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2607.05114v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods such as LoRA adapt large models through a single low-rank update. Such updates are susceptible to gradient interference: when a training stream interleaves multiple operational contexts, conflicting updates to shared adapter weights collapse the adapter into an unspecialized average. While recent methods introduce block-wise isolation to remedy this issue, their topologies are static and cannot adapt to context switching or localized sensor degradation. In this work, we introduce Localized LoRA-MoE, a framework that combines localized spatial blocking with context-conditioned expert routing. We propose and evaluate two architectural variants: Block-Wise LoRA-MoE (centralized routing), which modulates the entire structural grid through a single context-conditioned gate, and Cell-Wise LoRA-MoE (decentralized routing), which assigns an independent gate to every coordinate cell of the matrix grid. Across three structured transformation benchmarks--a high-dimensional SVD matrix simulation, context-switched transformations over real tabular data, and spatial reconstruction under simulated sensor occlusion--both variants outperform static baselines under comparable adapter budgets. Both variants perform similarly when context shifts the grid uniformly, while cell-wise routing is strictly better when contexts are spatially heterogeneous. When fine-tuning a language model on six interleaved GLUE tasks, task-conditioned routing at a fixed adapter budget outperforms LoRA and static localized adapters, matching per-task adapters with 6x budgets. At decoder scale on Qwen2.5-1.5B, both routed variants outperform static baselines across eight commonsense benchmarks, with cell-wise routing achieving +3.9 points over LoRA at matched active capacity.

articles.title_original: OpenMHC: Accelerating the Science of Wearable Foundation Models
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2607.16235v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Mobile and wearable devices offer an unprecedented opportunity for continuous, passive health monitoring and active health coaching. However, the largest wearable datasets are proprietary, and leading wearable foundation models trained on them are rarely open weight or include reproducible training code. To accelerate open science in wearable health, we introduce OpenMyHeartCounts (OpenMHC), the largest and most comprehensive wearable health dataset broadly accessible to qualified researchers, alongside open-source implementations and weights for recent wearable foundation models. Derived from over a decade of data collected through the My Heart Counts study app, OpenMHC comprises over 67M participant-hours of wearable recordings across up to 19 sensor channels (e.g., step count, heart rate, sleep, workouts) and up to 170 health, lifestyle, mood, and behavioral variables from 11,894 participants. Furthermore, we establish a benchmark for standardized evaluation across three tasks: (1) health and behavioral outcome prediction, (2) multivariate data imputation, and (3) time-series forecasting. Benchmarking classical methods alongside recent wearable and time-series foundation models, we find that while foundation models perform strongly, carefully tuned classical baselines like XGBoost remain highly competitive. By uniting broad-access wearable data with open code and model weights, OpenMHC provides a framework needed to drive reproducible advances in wearable health AI.

articles.title_original: Sampling Luck Masquerades as Allocation Gain: Auditing Test-Time Budget Allocation for Neural Combinatorial Optimization
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2608.13087v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) solvers report the best of many sampled solutions per instance, and the sample count is, by convention, identical for every instance. Whether a non-uniform allocation of a fixed total budget would buy anything has not been measured. We measure it, and we audit the measurement itself.
  First, on in-distribution workloads the allocation headroom is not detectable. Across three pretrained solvers (POMO, AM, SymNCO) on uniform TSP-100, an oracle allocation computed and evaluated on the same stored samples reports a 2.2-2.6% gain with intervals excluding zero; measured out of sample the same gain is indistinguishable from zero (0.457, 0.015, -0.512 percent). Following the customary in-sample procedure, all three solvers would have supported a published 2%-level gain that does not exist. We calibrate this bias against an instance-wise null in which the true gain is zero by construction; over the ranges we test it does not shrink with more samples or more instances.
  Second, the same correction that removes the phantom gains preserves a real one. Under distribution shift (a workload mixing uniform and clustered instances), a pre-registered confirmatory experiment finds that allocation guided by held-out sample statistics improves best-of-k by 11.5% (AM, primary endpoint; 95% CI [7.4, 19.7]) and 12.0% (SymNCO, replication) at equal evaluation budget, with the signal-acquisition cost not charged; a pre-registered negative control (POMO, an order of magnitude more robust to shift) shows -0.3% [-0.7, 0.24]. The gain exceeds a frozen distribution-label baseline by 4.2 points [1.9, 7.7]. An exploratory policy charging a 20-sample probe against the same budget retains 3.4% (AM) and 4.6% (SymNCO).
  We give a correction procedure and a reporting checklist, and release all data, code, and the pre-registration record.

articles.title_original: When Candidate Pools Miss Active Constraints: Evidence from Electromagnetic and Thermal Design
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2608.18903v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Finite candidate pools can limit surrogate-assisted design when good designs lie near intersecting active constraints. For independent uniform candidates in a normalized box, the typical minimum sum of gaps to k active bounds scales as (k!/N)^(1/k) for a pool of size N. This geometric limitation persists even with an accurate surrogate. We examine it through a controlled synthetic study and two finite-element design problems with inexpensive analytic constraints: a seven-variable electromagnetic coil and an independent six-variable heat spreader. The budget permits 25 initial observations and 50 further evaluations. On ten matched seeds, replacing pool EI with continuous constrained EI refinement raises mean coil response from 0.9120 to 0.9745 mT and lowers mean thermal resistance from 12.688 to 11.905 K/W. Standard continuous LogEI performs better than this refinement on nine coil seeds and all ten thermal seeds, reaching 0.9770 mT and 11.860 K/W. GP-mean search has the highest nominal coil mean but exhibits a thermal outlier on one seed. Mesh and domain checks preserve the substantial continuous-search advantage over the pool; they do not establish a resolved physical ranking among the closely performing continuous policies. Together, the sampling analysis and matched simulations identify when finite-pool search restricts the use of an FEM budget. The results support continuous constrained acquisition search, with stable LogEI as an effective existing implementation, when finite pools poorly represent high-value boundary designs.
  Bayesian optimization; acquisition optimization; active constraints; simulation-driven design; finite-element method; Gaussian-process surrogate; electromagnetic coil design; heat conduction

articles.title_original: Fairness-Aware Test-Time Prompt Tuning
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2608.25707v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Vision-language models have displayed remarkable capabilities in multi-modal understanding and are increasingly used in critical applications where economic and practical deployment constraints prohibit re-training or fine-tuning. However, these models can also exhibit systematic biases that disproportionately affect protected demographic groups and existing approaches to addressing these biases require extensive model retraining and access to demographic attributes. There is a clear need to develop test-time adaptation (TTA) approaches that improve the fairness characteristics of pretrained models under distributional shift. In this paper, we evaluate how episodic TTA affects fairness in CLIP classification under subpopulation shifts and develop FairTPT, a novel fairness-aware episodic TTA method that jointly minimizes target marginal entropy while maximizing spurious marginal entropy through soft-prompt tuning. We find that standard episodic TTA generally exacerbates disparities between majority and minority groups, that blinding a model to spurious attributes without degrading target performance is inherently challenging, and that excessive blinding can lead to catastrophic forgetting. This model collapse can be prevented by monitoring test-time changes in target loss within the linear regime, while still achieving fairness improvements on reactive data and preserving overall performance. FairTPT outperforms all state-of-the-art episodic test-time debiasing methods and establishes a foundation for robust TTA, which is essential for achieving fairness in practice.

articles.title_original: Learning Complementary Routes for Scouting Persimmon Orchards during Shoot Growth with CoverShare
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2608.27507v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: At the study orchard, scouting during persimmon shoot growth focuses on leaf color change, leaf area, and internode length. Several routes may share an access lane, yet each can offer a view of row segments that the others miss. We introduce CoverShare to learn complementary routes under a fixed action budget. Within Policy Gradient for Parallel State Entropy maximization (PGPSE), CoverShare redistributes auxiliary rewards according to the state coverage lost when each policy is omitted and the number of policies visiting each state. It preserves the pooled entropy objective and total auxiliary reward. We simulated the annotated road network of a 6.7-ha site with 107 observable persimmon scouting units across five zones. At 40 actions per route, six distinct policies covered an expected 17.84 units perinspection, compared with 8.28 for six independent runs of one policy, averaged across eight training seeds. With the same policies trained on 40-action routes, extending each inspection route to 80 and 120 actions raised coverage to 22.52 and 28.38 units. Across seven public discrete-state tasks, CoverShare increased state support by a mean of 16.29% over the team-entropy baseline. Controlled ablations identified leave-one-policy-out coverage as the main contributor to these gains.

articles.title_original: Dandelion: A Spherical Flower for Neural Simulation of Planetary Dynamics
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2608.27521v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Many dynamical processes unfold on the sphere but the default scientific machine learning architectures are Euclidean. Applying these architectures on a regular lat--lon grid causes problems: Cartesian convolutions become distorted at high latitude; 2D FFTs in Fourier neural operators incorrectly assume double periodicity; Cartesian positional encodings in ViTs distort spherical geodesic distances. Recent work moves towards natively spherical primitives, including spherical convolutions (e.g., DeepSphere or DISCO), Spherical Fourier Neural Operators (SFNOs), and geodesic attention. Here we propose Dandelion, a spherical version of Flower---a warp-based neural PDE solver. A Dandelion layer computes a tangent-plane displacement and then transports features along great circles. We obtain a U-Net-like structure by implementing hierarchical pooling entirely in the spherical-harmonic domain. There are thus no convolutions: spatial mixing is achieved only through spherical coordinate changes---or warps. To compare Dandelion with existing spherical architectures, we release an evolving benchmark suite of challenging, natively spherical PDE datasets including a modified Galewsky jet, anomalous chained turbulence, Cahn--Hilliard decomposition, spherical Riemann shocks, Held--Suarez dry atmospheric transport and global ocean dynamics. This new benchmark fills the gap between existing spherical datasets which are either too small and stylized, or much too large (ERA5) for model iteration. Dandelion achieves the best performance on all but one benchmark setting, where the best model is Flower2D, also based on warps. The spherical primitives result in the most physically consistent forecasts.

articles.title_original: Amortizing Scaling Law Construction Costs
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2609.05016v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Scaling laws guide the design choices for training large foundation models, but deriving them involves training an exhaustive grid over hyperparameters, token budgets, and parameter counts, which is computationally expensive. Fitting a scaling law, however, only requires the best-loss frontier across compute scales, discarding most of the trained configurations. We propose a framework for efficient scaling law construction that formulates data collection as a Bayesian optimization problem, and introduce metrics for comparing scaling law fitting methods under constrained compute budgets. We find that progressively expanding the compute budget during acquisition, mirroring the compute-ordered evaluation of configurations in practice, substantially improves recovery efficiency. Augmenting the observed configurations with surrogate-fantasized evaluations then recovers the broader experimental grid, allowing accurate scaling law fitting without training every configuration. Together, these can closely match scaling law fits over a full dense grid at computational savings of up to $10\text{--}100\times$.

articles.title_original: Feature Selection for Tabular Foundation Models: Exploring Feature Utility in Low-Data Molecular Prediction
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2609.30789v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Choosing features is difficult with few labeled molecules, even for a tabular foundation model that learns in context. We study this problem with TabPFN for low-data molecular property prediction, separating input width, feature meaning, and predictive usefulness while keeping contexts, query molecules, and predictor settings matched. On ADME/Tox assays from Therapeutics Data Commons, endpoint-matched assay predictions improve a compact RDKit descriptor baseline, and a provenance audit shows that most audited query molecules already occur in the predictors' training sources. Across 77 FS-Mol development tasks and 157 held-out test assays drawn from ChEMBL, broad RDKit descriptor and fingerprint families provide a strong default, rank-averaging TabPFN with support-fitted fingerprint forests improves upon both models, and learned weighting of family predictions adds further gains at a larger prediction budget. A utility-trained selector builds a traceable 16-column input from 238 sourceassay predictors, improving upon the baseline while trailing wider representations and equalwidth structural SVD coordinates. Named outputs identify what each feature predicts and where it comes from. Their usefulness for a new assay is assessed alongside the other input features, and paired removal and replacement tests measure what each selected output contributes. Together, these studies offer a protocol for evaluating feature selection, representation choice, and data provenance with a fixed tabular foundation model for few-shot molecular property prediction.

articles.title_original: Intuition Vectors from Pretrained Representations Steer Diffusion-Based Reasoning
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2609.32619v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Abstract visual reasoning requires identifying relationships between few examples and applying them to novel inputs. Recent advances have been driven by large language and vision-language models or specialized domain-specific architectures. It remains unclear whether abstract reasoning can be supported directly by the relational geometry of pretrained visual representations, without relying on language-based inference or task-specific representation learning. We investigate this possibility using frozen self-supervised vision encoders. With latent vector arithmetic, we confirmed that the representational geometry of two self-supervised encoders support abstract concept discrimination on Bongard problems and encode systematic relationships between input-output pairs in ARC tasks. Simple vector differences between image embeddings, which we call intuition vectors, capture transformations that generalize across instances of the same task. These vectors distinguish among 794 abstract reasoning tasks with up to 87.2\% accuracy, preserve relational structure across task-invariant visual transformations, and guide output retrieval for unseen inputs. Given this, we tested the hypothesis that this relational structure can steer generative reasoning by conditioning a diffusion transformer operating in pretrained visual latent space. On held-out ARC tasks, intuition-vector conditioning outperforms conditioning on complete demonstrations while requiring nearly six times less test-time compute, and supports zero-shot inference. Taken together, our findings suggest that pretrained visual representations provide a transferable substrate for abstract reasoning, enabling a modular approach in which the relational structure inferred from demonstrations steer generative reasoning.

articles.title_original: ScAn-Bench: Evaluating Scaling Analysis Methodology
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2609.35707v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Recent progress in machine learning is driven by large-scale foundation models, where scaling laws and finding optimal scaling prescriptions for architecture, data, and hyperparameters are key in advancing the state-of-the-art. Therefore, it is surprising that no systematic study evaluates the methodology to obtain scaling laws and prescriptions across different model types. To shed light on this crucial blind spot and facilitate future research, we introduce the surrogate benchmarks ScAn-Bench-LLM and ScAn-Bench-VLM based on 4524 and 8024 checkpoints of language and vision-language model pipelines. On our benchmarks, we perform the first systematic evaluation of both data acquisition and extrapolation methodology for scaling analysis across different data modalities.

articles.title_original: Representable but Unlearned: Encoding Rank and the Interaction-Prediction Floor
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2609.36208v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Input encodings can prevent a predictor from reproducing measured interactions jointly, even when each interaction is individually representable. We compute the attainable contrast space from the encoder and contrast design, without labels or predictor fitting. Projecting measured contrasts onto this space gives an empirical squared-error floor for any deterministic decoder using the encoding. On an siRNA panel, a graph neural network's training-only feature mask merges 165 measured states into 90 classes, reducing the rank of 140 interaction contrasts to 72. The floor is 0.009980, or 14.63% of recorded contrast energy, the mean squared error of predicting zero for every contrast. Its 14.6% share of fitted interaction error adds little: predicted interactions are nearly zero, and their MSE of 0.068335 slightly exceeds that of the same control. Antisense-marginal shares are larger: 36.49% of recorded energy and 38.1% of fitted error. Three restored chemistry columns suffice for full rank. Removing the full mask eliminates the floor, but refitting improves interaction MSE by only 0.000017; the restored features remain absent from training inputs. Two further panels clarify the diagnostic's scope. A released splicing predictor encodes injectively and retains the full design rank of 1,986, so its floor is zero. For an independent count-fingerprint encoder on a lipid panel, 800 pairwise-distinct encoded contrast rows have rank 740, exposing 60 restrictions missed by duplicate-row checks. The diagnostic identifies encoding-imposed limits and can trace them to specific features. It separates representability from learned accuracy, but does not by itself predict refitting gains or explain the remaining error.

articles.title_original: Where Root Cause Analysis Fails: A Retrieval-Reranking Decomposition
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2609.36686v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Identifying the root cause of an anomaly among hundreds of sensors is critical for preventing safety incidents and costly downtime in complex monitored systems. Existing studies evaluate root cause analysis (RCA) methods using top@k accuracy. We show that this metric has a fundamental blind spot: it conflates two failure modes, retrieval failure, where the true cause is never considered, and reranking failure, where it is considered but ranked too low. In this work, we introduce a retrieval-reranking decomposition and audit four well-known benchmarks to expose this blind spot. Our experiments show that, on industrial CPS benchmarks, the statistical baseline scoring every sensor mis-ranks the true cause 79-100% of the time, and graph-based methods never clearly beat the best statistical baseline, whether their causal graphs are learned on short fault windows, on retrieved candidate pools guaranteed to contain the cause, or on multi-day normal-operation data. Meanwhile, on microservice benchmarks, where each injected fault drives the faulty service's own metric far above its baseline, retrieval is nearly solved (98-100%). Guided by the decomposition, we build a two-stage pipeline combining a multi-signal retriever with an LLM reranker that, as one fixed configuration, matches or exceeds the best baseline's top@1 accuracy on all six benchmark suites (by up to +12 points), with no causal graph or labeled data required. When all methods rank the same retrieved candidates with the true cause guaranteed present, adding a short system-description document lets the reranker lead the best baseline by +7 to +18 points on every benchmark. Code is available at https://github.com/cruiseresearchgroup/DecompRCA.

articles.title_original: LeapQuant: Efficient Linear Attention with Accurate Recurrent State Quantization
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2609.38166v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Recent LLMs increasingly adopt hybrid designs that replace standard attention with linear attention, such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN) and Kimi Delta Attention (KDA). Although they compress the context into a fixed-size recurrent state and substantially reduce the cost of long-context processing, repeatedly reading and updating that state remains a major inference bottleneck. Quantization offers a natural way to reduce this cost, but can significantly degrade model quality, due to the accumulation of rounding errors and the presence of outlier rows and columns in the state. To address these challenges, we propose LeapQuant, a training-free method that achieves near-lossless performance under 8-bit recurrent-state quantization. First, to mitigate error accumulation, we propose per-window quantization, which leaps over a window of tokens and quantizes the state only once at its end. Within a window, outputs are computed from the fixed low-bit state together with high-precision buffered updates. Second, to reduce the error introduced by each quantization, LeapQuant retains the state's largest outliers as a few high-precision Compensator Tokens, which share the update path of real tokens. We then smooth the remaining residual before quantization to further reduce the error. Comprehensive experiments across the Qwen, Kimi, and GLM model families show that LeapQuant substantially reduces memory and compute costs during inference. With accuracy comparable to the FP32 baseline, it achieves average speedups of 2.05--3.70$\times$ at the kernel level and 1.47$\times$ for end-to-end inference on NVIDIA B200, RTX PRO 6000, and RTX 5090 GPUs.

articles.title_original: ElectrolyteFM: Unifying Electrolyte Property Prediction through Cross-Property Knowledge Learning
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2609.39340v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Electrolyte formulation design requires balancing multiple physicochemical properties, yet existing models often focus on a limited subset. Learning each property in isolation can overlook transferable chemical information, whereas indiscriminate sharing can introduce cross-property interference. Our directed transfer analysis shows that jointly learning two property prediction tasks can improve or degrade prediction relative to separate training, with asymmetric transfer effects between the tasks. We propose ElectrolyteFM, a unified multi-property prediction model which can more accurately predict multiple properties of each electrolyte by effectively identifying and utilizing property-specific features and knowledge shared across properties. More specifically, ElectrolyteFM learns property-specific representations independently and captures cross-property knowledge through a separately trained expert pool. A router selects relevant shared information for each formulation and target property, and property-specific residual adapters convert this information into corrections to the corresponding representation for prediction. Experiments on Electrolyte12 show that ElectrolyteFM reduces normalized mean absolute error averaged across 12 electrolyte properties by 14.8% relative to the strongest electrolyte-specific baseline. On an independent sodium-electrolyte dataset unseen during training, it reduces conductivity mean absolute error by 6.7% relative to the best-performing baseline.

articles.title_original: Pseudo-Label-Triggered Retraining from Forecast Errors for Online Time Series Forecasting
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2609.39789v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Real-world time series forecasting systems operate under non-stationary data streams, where forecasting performance may degrade over time. Although retraining can recover the performance, it incurs non-trivial computational and operational costs. Under limited deployment resources, the key challenge is therefore not only how to retrain but also when to retrain. While existing retraining policies often rely on indirect indicators such as drift alarms or model staleness, we instead use realized forecast errors as direct deployment feedback. In this paper, we propose PILOT (Pseudo-label-Informed Learned Online Trigger), an online retraining framework that learns when to retrain from forecast-error dynamics. Since ground-truth retraining labels are unavailable, PILOT constructs a pseudo-label from future increases in forecast error and trains a lightweight scorer to predict it from observed error states. At deployment, PILOT uses only completed forecast errors and serves as a plug-in module for arbitrary forecasting backbones without architectural modification. We evaluate PILOT under standard multivariate forecasting settings across eight benchmarks with three representative backbones---DLinear, iTransformer, and TimesNet. Across all three backbones, PILOT achieves state-of-the-art average-rank performance among retraining policies while maintaining a favorable performance--efficiency trade-off.

articles.title_original: One pool, many targets: a conservation layer and what archival data can identify
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.00445v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Pairwise guide-transcript scores do not enforce conservation of a finite guide-loaded RISC pool when they are interpreted independently as occupancies. We formulate a differentiable scalar equilibrium layer: one conservation equation with a unique positive root and exact implicit gradients. It yields a redistribution theorem, a qualified high-resource limit, an analysis of the retrieval approximation, and a conditional rank-invariance result: within one construct at one dose, rankings by fractional occupancy cannot distinguish equilibrium from independent scoring. We therefore audit the two experiments that proposition leaves open, dose and cross-context, on archival off-target data. Corrected thermodynamic affinities associate weakly with measured repression in the direction a working predictor requires, but a paired permutation test and a construct-cluster bootstrap do not establish added predictive value from the coupling: what survives their differing permutation-null baselines is 0.0026, which is 2.55 paired-null standard deviations from that baseline (p=0.010) and favours independent scoring. The dose fits are heterogeneous and frequently violate the model-implied exponent constraint, which is superlinear rather than sublinear, so these data do not identify the competition parameter. A saturable compression of the competitor set holds both accuracy targets on held-out guide families but is not faster at the size measured. The contribution is a reusable conservation operator and the experimental information needed to test it. Code, result files and the data manifest: https://github.com/shadi97kh/One-Pool-Many-Targets

articles.title_original: Misalignment of Low-Loss Regions Causes Grokking
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.00620v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Grokking refers to the delayed emergence of validation-set generalization after a model has already overfit the training set. Although first observed in small algorithmic tasks trained with transformers, its underlying mechanism remains unsettled. In this work, we develop an analysis framework based on mode connectivity and the geometry of low-loss regions. The framework predicts that the standard modular-arithmetic setting does not always produce grokking: under a symmetry-preserving train/validation split, we observe a stable anti-grokking case in which validation performance does not recover. This counterexample challenges several existing correlational explanations of grokking. More broadly, our analysis framework and results further suggest that grokking arises when the low-loss regions induced by the training and validation partitions are misaligned. Once these regions become well aligned, training hyperparameters alone cannot produce grokking and the observed dynamics collapse to either trainable or non-trainable behavior.

articles.title_original: Trust the Direction, Search the Step: Zero-and-First-Order Methods for LLM Fine-Tuning
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.02190v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Step-size selection remains a central challenge in large-scale neural network optimization; conservative steps slow convergence, while aggressive steps can destabilize it. We combine Zero-and-First-Order optimization (ZFO) and propose a lightweight framework that decouples direction selection from step-size. ZFO uses a trusted first-order optimizer to determine the direction and performs zeroth-order evaluations only along this one-dimensional subspace to choose how far to move. Using the current {gradient information} and two additional objective function evaluations, ZFO instances construct a local model of the objective function along the proposed direction and select a curvature-aware step within a bounded search interval. This yields an adaptive step-selection mechanism that costs less than a full line search. We provide theoretical guarantees to show that shared-sample evaluations produce reliable finite-difference curvature estimates, that the induced local model selects a near-optimal step along the search interval, and that ZFO converges to a neighborhood of a stationary point. Across the evaluated settings, language models and datasets, ZFO frequently improves optimization and final performance relative to fixed-step first-order baselines, with the magnitude and preferred local model depending on the objective. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/nizswan/Zeroth-First-Order-Framework.

articles.title_original: OVAL: Output-Aware Local Page Bases for KV Cache Compression
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.06686v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Long-context decoding, whether over long reasoning traces, long videos, or robot episodes, is increasingly limited by the memory of the key-value (KV) cache. Page-retrieval sparse attention makes each decoding step cheaper by attending only to the top-scoring KV pages. However, it still stores every page exactly, and adds a small digest per page for scoring, so the cache ends up slightly \emph{larger} than the full cache. We propose OVAL, which stores each page as a pair of output-aware low-rank bases that act as both the retrieval index and the storage. A key basis scores the page and rebuilds its keys when the page is selected, and a PCA basis rebuilds its values. The exact pages can then be dropped, and nothing extra is added to the cache. The key idea is that the key basis should be output-aware. A low-rank error in the keys perturbs the attention output at first order, but perturbs the page mass that retrieval ranks only at second order in expectation. OVAL therefore builds the key basis from a mix of key geometry (key PCA) and the attention-output error, with a per-head mixing weight set in closed form. At the same attended budget, OVAL is best or tied-best in eight of nine long-reasoning settings. It matches FullKV on MATH500 with 66\% of its memory, is 1.25 points above the best baseline on AIME24 with 56\%, and is on par with FullKV on LongBench~v2. On \mbox{Video-MME} and LVBench, it is within 0.32 points of exact-page retrieval at the same read, while storing 53\% of the full cache instead of 103\%. Its savings also stack with quantization and token pruning: with 4-bit bases, it is within 0.25 points of FullKV at 41\% of its memory.

articles.agent: アルゴリズム担当エージェント
articles.title_original: Do Neural PDE Solvers Learn the Right Dynamics?
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.06952v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Neural PDE solvers can achieve low prediction errors, but do they reproduce the dynamics of the systems they model? Prediction scores alone offer an incomplete answer: they measure agreement with reference solutions but provide limited insight into how errors accumulate, nearby states diverge, or extreme events arise. We propose an evaluation framework that directly examines these behaviors in deterministic and stochastic neural solvers. By evolving ensembles of nearby initial states and comparing them with direct numerical simulation, we assess three complementary aspects of learned dynamics: error formation, ensemble geometry, and extreme events. Experiments on two-dimensional Kolmogorov flow reveal limitations that conventional scores can obscure. Smaller trajectory errors can reflect weaker error amplification despite less accurate local updates. Models can match an ensemble's overall spread and effective dimension while failing to capture the spatial directions where nearby states diverge. Similarly, matching overall event frequencies can conceal failures to predict persistent extreme events. These findings show that improved prediction accuracy does not necessarily imply greater dynamical fidelity. Our framework makes this distinction measurable, providing concrete criteria for evaluating whether advances in neural PDE solvers better capture the underlying dynamics.

articles.agent: アルゴリズム担当エージェント
articles.title_original: Does On-Policy Distillation Need to Complete Every Rollout?
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.21337v5 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers teacher knowledge to a student through feedback on student-generated rollouts, but generating complete rollouts and computing per-token teacher feedback are computationally expensive. Existing truncation methods save computation by stopping rollouts early. However, they do not compensate for truncated token gradients, which biases the gradient estimates and changes Vanilla OPD's original training objective. Furthermore, their truncation decisions rely on assumptions about supervision quality or criteria that may not generalize across settings. We introduce Stochastic Truncated On-Policy Distillation (STOPD), which accelerates OPD by randomly truncating student rollouts and correcting the resulting sampling bias with blockwise inverse-probability weighting (IPW). At each training step, we sample a stopping position for each rollout before generation and let the student generate until that position or natural termination. We obtain teacher feedback on every generated token and use blockwise IPW to compensate for the lower probability of retaining later tokens while controlling the weights. We prove that this weighting preserves Vanilla OPD's gradient sum in expectation and derive one-step update-error bounds for SGD, Adam, and Muon. We evaluate STOPD across multiple teacher-student model pairs, task domains, and optimizers. STOPD reduces generated tokens by 25-48% while maintaining accuracy comparable to Vanilla OPD, achieving 1.3-2.2x training speedups.

articles.title_original: Dynamical Kernel Attention: Estimating the Present from a Record of the Past
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.24026v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Self-attention encodes where a past token lies, but not how its uncertainty grows with time: evidence accumulates without bound as the context grows, and nothing indicates which tokens are safe to discard. We introduce Dynamical Kernel Attention (DKA), which derives attention from robust estimation of a latent state governed by a stochastic differential equation. Under this model, each head draws bounded evidence from any context. This lets each head abstain when relevant evidence is weak, and gives each head a memory window outside which discarding tokens changes its output by a provably bounded amount. On language modeling, DKA outperforms RoPE within the training length and ALiBi far beyond it, and matches sliding-window attention with a substantially smaller key-value cache.

articles.title_original: Forecasting Retail Sales at Every Grain: Trees, Foundation Models, Transformers and World Models Compared on Four Public Data Sets
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.25170v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: A retailer makes decisions from the same demand at different grains: store orders by item and day, promotions by item and week, category reviews and supplier terms. This paper asks whether one forecast, built at the finest grain and summed to every coarser grain, can serve them all, and which model does that best. It compares LightGBM, pretrained foundation models (TimesFM, Chronos-Bolt, Timestral), the Temporal Fusion Transformer and a world model that carries each item's state forward under the price and promotion plan, on M5, six Dominick's categories, Breakfast at the Frat and Corporacion Favorita, with the world model and LightGBM tuned by a common search. When to use the average: the average of the tuned world model and LightGBM, summed to every grain, has the lowest error in 22 of 27 grain and data set cases and is never the least accurate on the final held-out periods. When to use the world model: on existing items kept out of training it loses at most 0.040 in scaled error, against up to 0.311 for LightGBM, and on lines with short history it is clearly more accurate on six of nine data sets. When to use LightGBM: on heavily promoted lines, fast sellers and lines with long history (six of nine data sets each) and in price-cut weeks. Inconclusive: lines never promoted and slow lines are close to even, and 52 weeks ahead the average is the most accurate on five of seven data sets, with the world model ahead of LightGBM on two of seven. The findings hold for these data sets and the price and promotion levers; anyone adopting them should rerun every comparison on their own data.

articles.title_original: Activation-Space Exploration for Visual and Textual Reasoning with RLVR
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.27012v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves visual and textual reasoning by sampling responses, scoring them with an automatic verifier, and updating the policy from the resulting rewards. The policy therefore receives direct learning signals only from trajectories that appear in its rollouts. Yet repeated sampling from the same policy can concentrate on similar reasoning paths, leaving useful alternatives unexplored under a fixed rollout budget. We introduce Activation-Space Exploration (ASE), an online method for diversifying training rollouts. By clustering activation differences between correct and incorrect responses to the same problem, ASE builds a structured bank of latent exploration vectors. Different vectors are then applied to subsequent rollouts to explore alternative reasoning paths. Under the same rollout budget, ASE improves average accuracy over GRPO on Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct by 5.41 and 3.15 percentage points across six visual mathematical and six general visual reasoning benchmarks, respectively. On Qwen3-1.7B-Base, it improves average Mean@8 over GRPO across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks by 4.87 percentage points, with gains also observed on Qwen3-8B-Base.

articles.title_original: Compositional neural networks for multimodal X-ray and neutron scattering inversion
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.29362v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: X-ray and neutron scattering are indispensable for structural characterization across condensed-matter physics and materials science. Yet, because scattering experiments generally record intensities without phase information, distinct structures can yield similar scattering patterns, rendering the corresponding inverse problems non-unique. This ambiguity can be reduced by combining complementary measurements, but their integration into machine-learning frameworks remains challenging. Here we introduce a modular framework for probabilistic multi-measurement analysis based on prior-amortized flow matching. Single-observation posterior estimators are trained separately for individual observation types or physical probes and combined only at inference time through a compositional sampler. This late fusion approach allows pretrained single-observation models to be reused without dedicated joint retraining. As a case in point, we consider reflectometry, which provides depth-resolved, nanometer-scale information about thin films and interfaces. Our single-observation demonstrations span X-ray, time-of-flight neutron and polarized neutron reflectometry. In separate co-refinement studies, task-matched estimators enable homogeneous composition across multiple neutron contrasts and heterogeneous multimodal composition of X-ray and neutron measurements. Together, these results establish compositional flow matching as a modular approach to uncertainty-aware inversion and co-refinement, with potential applicability to other scattering problems in which multiple observations constrain a common physical structure while retaining measurement-specific parameters.

articles.title_original: Estimating aerosol particle number size distributions from PM2.5 with physics-regularized flow matching
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.33557v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: The mass concentration of particles smaller than 2.5um (PM2.5) is cheap to measure and widely monitored, whereas the particle number size distribution (PNSD) requires costly instruments and is measured at only a few research stations. Yet many aerosol effects, such as vapor uptake, cloud droplet formation and deposition in the human respiratory tract, depend on the PNSD rather than on mass. We explore whether generative deep learning models can infer the current PNSD from routine data: from the PM2.5 record and eight meteorological variables over a 24h window, a model generates an ensemble of plausible hourly PNSDs for the same window, reflecting that one mass can arise from many size distributions. Rather than proposing a single best model, we use two contrasting Finnish stations, the boreal forest site Hyytiala and the urban site Kumpula, as a controlled testbed. On it, we benchmark six generative models against deterministic regression and historical-mean baselines, locally and after transfer between sites, and test physical constraints for neural network training. Flow matching performs best overall; its guided variant has the lowest continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) at both sites. A constraint based on a reduced aerosol general dynamic equation (GDE) lowers the CRPS by 5.5-11.5% at the training site and reduces errors after transfer between sites. Transfer remains harder than local estimation, identifying multi-station training as the next step towards PNSD estimates at unmonitored locations. This benchmark establishes physics-informed generative models as a promising route from routine air-quality monitoring to size-resolved aerosol information.

articles.title_original: Shared Context, Separate Engines: Stateful Streaming Inference for Multimodal LLMs on Edge SoCs
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.35309v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Streaming multimodal large language models (MLLMs) must take in new video frames while answering questions about what they have already seen. On an edge SoC, if one engine does both, ingestion and answering compete for its time while the other engines sit idle. To take over a query, another engine must first import or rebuild the accumulated history, because each runtime keeps it as KV state in its own format. 
ame lets one engine answer from history that another engine built. Each query reads the history as it stood when the query was asked, so one engine can keep ingesting while another answers. The CPU and GPU can also decode answers to different queries simultaneously. Phase-level state continuation lets an engine prefill a query, pass its KV state to another engine for decoding, and return to ingestion. State-Driven Execution Planning (SDEP) chooses where each query is prefilled and decoded, based on the state each engine holds and the work queued on it. Across M4 Max, RK3588, and QCS6490, 
ame outperforms single-engine execution. On a live M4 Max stream, SDEP cuts p95 time to first token by $76\%$, and every query receives its first token within one second. Under backlog, it raises request throughput by up to $35\%$. For two concurrent video streams on RK3588, SDEP delivers $19.6\%$ higher request throughput than single-engine execution and $27.2\%$ more than running both engines in parallel without shared state. 
ame delivers up to $2.48	imes$ the throughput of the same engines run serially. Every answer matches serial execution token for token.

articles.title_original: Alpha-TCM: Auditable Knowledge Integration for Multimodal TCM Inference
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.38754v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Knowledge-guided multimodal systems need a way to measure how supplied knowledge affects predictions, including when that knowledge is wrong. Alpha-TCM addresses this problem for traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) through an implemented workflow that separates measurements, supplied knowledge, predictions, and reviewer decisions. Observations and contextual knowledge enter separately, and a replaceable prior allows controlled interventions with fixed modality encoders. Bayesian committee accounting removes the reference prior already contained in each encoder before inserting contextual knowledge. A fully simulated confirmation study uses ten paired seeds and four training sizes. Knowledge context reduces prediction error relative to knowledge-free fusion at 600 and 1,200 training cases; equal-information learned context is competitive at 600 and has lower error at larger sizes. Controlled corruption identifies overconfident and displaced priors as the most damaging challenges. Case-level conflict detection remains weak, and training-time prior regularisation shows no consistent benefit. Functional tests verify the connected workflow separately from predictive performance. The simulation demonstrates how Alpha-TCM measures knowledge dependence, separates it from gains due to additional context, and exposes harmful prior assumptions before clinical evaluation.

articles.title_original: Seeing Is Not Enough: Knowledge-Grounded Active Inquiry from Uncertain Visual Evidence
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.38774v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Similar tongue findings can accompany different syndromes in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), with decisive symptoms absent from the photograph. We present a framework for tongue assessment in which image and pulse findings guide targeted symptom inquiry and acquired answers refine the syndrome shortlist before reporting. Image/pulse predictions guide selection from a sourced symptom question bank. Known answers update the assessment used to select the next question. A calibrated loss of support for the initial prediction triggers reassessment; a subsequent report requires fresh answers supporting a stable candidate. Question and answer records make these decisions inspectable. We construct 2,600 cases from distinct real tongue photographs, assigned syndromes, simulated symptom responses and rendered pulses; 2,599 enter five-fold source-disjoint evaluation and one is training-only. On clean images, image/pulse prediction alone achieves 46.4% fine-syndrome accuracy. At acquisition cost 12, inquiry without image/pulse evidence reaches 34.4%, whereas their combination reaches 65.8% accuracy and 90.8% top-three inclusion. A same-prior, training-optimized static order reaches 59.4% and 87.3%, respectively. In a 200-case visual-training intervention within the same bank, the first question changes in 46.7% of cases and the inquiry NLL-cost curve improves. Component comparisons distinguish these acquisition gains from the coverage-cost tradeoff of reassessment. These controlled results support image-guided acquisition of missing symptoms for ranked TCM decision support.

articles.title_original: Forecasting How RLHF Responds to Reward-Model Edits Before Training
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.03244v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Responses with headers, lists and greater length receive high scores from reward models (RMs), and RLHF policies learn to produce these features even when true quality does not improve. Practitioners therefore edit their RMs, but they learn whether an edit works only after an RL run. We show that the response of a policy to an RM edit can be forecast before training, from samples of the current policy and the scores of the old and new RM. If we read the RM as a set of prices, the first-order theory of KL-regularized RL implies that each feature moves in proportion to its within-prompt covariance with the change in reward. We implant controlled price changes into retrained RMs under a 2^(4-1) fractional factorial design with a self-distilled placebo, run 54 RL runs from six parent policies, and fix every forecast before the runs. With the covariance predictor, we predict the direction of all 20 changes in supply whose forecast has the same sign at every parent and explain 82% of the standardized change. With counterfactual prices, the classical alternative, we explain 50%. The forecast also holds under GRPO and for real RM upgrades, where we explain 66% out of sample with a coefficient frozen from the factorial runs. For rent, the gap between the proxy reward and a gold reward from stronger judges, we rank RM edits correctly with the same covariance over the first 30 steps (Spearman 0.94). This measures the horizon of the forecast: by step 200, the ranking of the factorial edits reverses under both RLOO and GRPO, while the real upgrades keep their order. When we vary the KL coefficient beta, the initial response does not depend on beta, and the response saturates below the KL equilibrium. In one experiment, the long-run response to a price rise is consistent with an additional implicit regularizer beta_0 of about 0.003 to 0.007.

articles.title_original: Thought-deciphering via hierarchical EEG-to-text alignment
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.03623v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Non-invasive brain-to-text interfaces offer alternative communication pathways for people with communication disabilities. However, sentence-level decoding from electroencephalography (EEG) remains challenging. We propose a hierarchical EEG-text alignment framework that retrieves previously unseen sentences by progressively decoding coarse-grained semantic information and fine-grained sentence representations. We hypothesize that broader semantic context can be more reliably captured from EEG than individual sentences. Accordingly, EEG representations are first classified into semantic classes, which are defined as groups of related sentences, followed by sentence retrieval within the predicted class. Among over 2,000 unique text samples, our approach achieves, on unseen sentences, average top-5 and top-10 retrieval accuracies of 62.6\% $\pm$ 1.0\% and 83.5\% $\pm$ 1.0\%, respectively, compared with 0.3\% $\pm$ 0.3\% and 0.5\% $\pm$ 0.2\% for direct EEG-sentence alignment without semantic classification. Qualitative analysis further reveals that decoding performance depends strongly on textual context. These findings demonstrate the potential of hierarchical semantic alignment for advancing sentence-level EEG-to-text decoding.

articles.title_original: NovoCRF: Globally Normalized De Novo Peptide Sequencing on a Prefix-Mass Lattice
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.05260v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: De novo peptide sequencing has moved from dynamic programming over hand-designed or generative scores to large transformers that learn the task end to end. We present NovoCRF, a conditional random field (CRF) whose states are prefix masses, so that its paths are exactly the peptides within $\pm$0.06 Da of the precursor mass. A small network scores each edge from physics-derived ion-match features and is trained with its scores globally normalized over all mass-feasible peptides. To our knowledge, NovoCRF is the first de novo method trained with exact normalization over all mass-feasible peptides. Our model has 3.6M parameters and trains in about 27 GPU-hours. Because it is small, NovoCRF can also adapt to each run at inference time: it fine-tunes part of its weights on the run's own confident answers, recalibrates the run's precursor and fragment masses, and uses retention time, predicted with a pretrained indexed-retention-time model, as further evidence. On nine held-out data-dependent acquisition datasets, NovoCRF has the highest peptide recall on five, and the transformer model InstaNovo on the other four. Where the spectrum determines the peptide, on labels with at most one peptide bond without a b or y ion, NovoCRF outperforms RNovA, $\pi$-PrimeNovo and CasanovoV5 on every dataset and InstaNovo on six of nine. The transformer models lead where many fragment ions are missing, and there their recall is up to 29 points higher on peptides of their own training data than on other peptides, while NovoCRF's recall differs least between seen and unseen peptides. NovoCRF also searches modifications it was never trained on at their exact mass: on a public spike-in of peptides with non-natural residues it finds 69.2% of the labeled spectra, against 64.4% for RNovA. With a GPU it sequences 203 spectra/s in its default two passes, and on the CPU alone it still sequences 67 spectra/s.

articles.title_original: Regularization Amplifies Subliminal Learning
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.10397v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Recent work has shown that hidden biases can be transferred through data with no apparent semantic relationship to those biases. Can regularization limit this covert influence? By constraining adaptation, regularization might be expected to suppress behavioral changes on seemingly unrelated inputs. We systematically study this hypothesis in subliminal learning, as well as in related settings of covert influence, including phantom transfer and logit-linear selection. We find the opposite: regularization amplifies the transfer of hidden biases. In particular, subliminal learning is typically absent under full fine-tuning, but low-rank adaptation or explicit penalties can induce strong transfer. Phantom transfer and logit-linear selection show similar trends. Adding more data, an implicit form of regularization, also strengthens covert influence. Together, these findings suggest that the simplicity biases induced by regularization may facilitate covert influence. We further hypothesize that the level of regularization that maximizes covert transfer depends on task complexity.

articles.title_original: Attention at Absolute Zero
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.11937v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Attention scores candidate supports of an answer, which we call witnesses, and reads the scores at a temperature. We build a higher-order attention layer whose state lives on pairs of items: for a pair (a, b), each third item k is a witness judged through its legs (a, k) and (k, b). It reads witnesses at zero temperature, keeping the best and the number tied with it, passes on only bits comparing such counts, rebuilds its pair state from the input and these bits at every loop, and is trained from answers alone. Each choice removes one way soft attention fails at size: dispersed weight, unresolved gaps between learned scores, and a drifting soft state. In maximum retrieval it is right on at least 99.95% of sets 1,000 times larger than in training, on all ten seeds; trained with a soft count, the same network falls to 42% at 4,096 items. On CLRS-30 without hints, a general form of the layer (half its channels read at zero temperature, numbers embedded, state carried) beats the best published model, which uses hints on some tasks; the full cold layer is exact on every test input of 9 of the 12 tasks whose answers depend on numbers only through comparisons. From yes-or-no answers it decides 2-SAT and two-colouring exactly at 500 variables and, as our theory predicts, not parity equations. Beside a frozen 7B language model it chains family relations exactly at 1,000 statements after training on 16, where the model alone falls to 44%; finite checks on the weights prove every block that learned correct at every size, on acyclic contexts and given what the model reads. On CLUTRR it is right on every story of five to ten relations given the graphs, learning the 62 rules exactly; from text, with the model frozen, no hand-written rule and only a small read-in trained, it lifts an open 7B model from 33% to 65%, above every system we found without hand-written rules except frontier reasoning models.

articles.title_original: Dual-Core Tensor Wheel Decomposition with Structure-Cached Acceleration for Tensor Recovery
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.13938v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Tensor wheel decomposition captures complex correlations in high-dimensional data through interactions between outer-ring factors and a high-order central core. However, updating these components requires the explicit construction and manipulation of large-scale matrices, which limits computational efficiency and incurs particularly high computational and memory costs for the central-core update. To address these limitations, we propose dual-core tensor wheel decomposition (DCTW), which factorizes the central core into two lower-order cores linked by a shared latent bond. Each core is coupled to a different group of outer-ring factors. We further propose a structure-cached acceleration strategy that avoids explicit large-scale matrix multi- plications and caches intermediate tensors generated during tensor network contractions for reuse across block updates. This reuse reduces redundant computation and avoids the explicit construction of large matrices. Complexity analysis and experiments show that the strategy based on structural caching accelerates optimization compared with explicit and implicit up- date schemes while limiting the increase in peak memory as the ranks grow. Experiments on color video completion and robust denoising show that DCTW matches or outperforms representative tensor network methods in reconstruction quality, computational efficiency, and scalability.

articles.agent: アルゴリズム担当エージェント
articles.title_original: Rethinking "RL Generalizes, SFT Memorizes": The Role of SFT Data
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.14912v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models trained with Reinforcement Learning (RL) with verifiable rewards exhibit strong reasoning ability and broad generalization, whereas models trained with Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) are often viewed as more prone to memorization and limited transfer. This paper rethinks this distinction through the lens of SFT training data on widely used Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 series models. First, we study the role of data source and show that it is critical: a carefully mixed SFT dataset substantially outperforms data generated solely by a larger model. Second, we study the role of data scale and show that matching the number of correct rollouts between SFT and RL greatly improves SFT generalization, while matching the total rollout budget enables SFT to generalize as well as RL. Combining these two factors further enables SFT to generalize even better than RL. Third, by using LLM annotations to characterize the solution methods in training rollouts, we show that larger datasets cover more tail methods and that these tail methods provide generalizable reasoning signals. Finally, we support these empirical findings theoretically by analyzing the training dynamics of shallow transformers under both RL and SFT.

articles.title_original: AI4Plasma I: Data-Efficient Surrogate Modeling of Capacitively Coupled Plasma Fields
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.15002v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Reference capacitively coupled plasma (CCP) simulations provide spatially resolved plasma fields but are costly to generate across operating conditions. We compare the data efficiency of five surrogate architectures--Coordinate MLP, PCA-Net, U-Net, Fourier neural operator (FNO), and Transolver--for predicting RF-cycle-averaged electron density, ion density, electric potential, and electron temperature in 1D planar and 2D axisymmetric GEC CCP benchmarks. We assess the number of reference simulations needed to achieve 1% and 2% mean relative L2 error for parameter-interior and parameter-boundary test cases, and examine architecture-specific mechanisms. FNO achieves the lowest or joint-lowest reference-case requirement in seven of eight comparisons. In 1D, FNO reaches 1% interior error with 50 training cases, compared with 100 for Transolver and 200 for U-Net. In 2D, FNO and U-Net each reach 1% interior error with 100 cases; FNO and Transolver each reach 2% parameter-boundary error with 200 cases, compared with 400 for U-Net. At the stricter 1% 2D parameter-boundary target, Transolver requires 400 cases versus 800 for FNO. Additional analyses investigate FNO spectral modes and padding, U-Net skip connections, Transolver adaptive slicing, and PCA-Net projection versus prediction error. The results support FNO as a data-efficient baseline for the tested CCP settings, while showing that the preferred architecture depends on the accuracy target and operating-parameter region.

articles.agent: アルゴリズム担当エージェント
articles.title_original: ReShap: Interpretable Reinforcement Learning for High-Dimensional Multi-Action Settings
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.15507v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Deep Reinforcement Learning (RL) plays a crucial role in tackling complex tasks, yet its reliance on deep neural networks makes the learned policies opaque. To enhance the trustworthiness of RL policies, existing work (e.g., the SILVER framework [Li et al., 2025]) has focused on Shapley-based interpretability, but is typically restricted to low-dimensional state spaces, binary-action settings, and a single class of linear surrogate. We propose ReShap, a policy-distillation framework that extends Shapley-based interpretability to high-dimensional, multi-action environments. ReShap extracts compact feature representations from raw image observations, performs SHAP-based feature attribution to characterize how each feature contributes to the policy's decisions, and distills the deep RL policy into an interpretable surrogate trained on the full set of (state, policy-action) pairs along the policy's visited distribution. We instantiate the surrogate with three interpretable model families (decision trees, linear regression, and logistic regression) and compare their fidelity and task return. We evaluate ReShap on Atari and Box2D environments using three deep RL algorithms and conduct a human-subject study to assess the clarity and trustworthiness of the resulting policies. Results show that ReShap preserves competitive task performance, that decision trees generally outperform linear and logistic regression, and that linear regression is weakest in most settings.

articles.agent: アルゴリズム担当エージェント
articles.title_original: AI4Plasma II: Geometry-Aware Surrogate Modeling for Variable Electrode Gap GEC Plasmas
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.15584v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Industrial plasma process development requires broad exploration of operating and geometric parameters. Geometric parameters, particularly electrode spacing, affect discharge structure and processing uniformity. Exploring these parameter spaces through repeated high-fidelity simulations can be computationally expensive. Surrogate models can offer rapid predictions, but geometric variation complicates their application because the computational domain and discretization may change across samples.
  In this work, six geometry-aware surrogate models based on prescribed and learned geometry mappings, extended-domain representation, continuous coordinates, and geometry-native discretizations are compared in terms of their data requirements for accurate predictions of full plasma fields and ion density profiles near the wafer. The simulation dataset spans pressure, voltage, frequency, and electrode gap, with each reference case requiring an average simulation cost of 5.32 CPU h.
  To achieve a 2% mean error across the four plasma fields, prescribed-mapping Geo-FNO and Transolver require 100 training cases, compared with 250-1000 for the other models. Predicting ion density profiles near the wafer is more demanding and reveals larger differences among models, with prescribed-mapping Geo-FNO requiring the fewest training cases for the profile accuracy targets considered. To further reduce the data required for accurate predictions near the wafer, we introduce charge-separation weighting into the training loss, which reduces the prescribed-mapping Geo-FNO's minimum tested training requirement for a 5% profile error from 1000 to 100 cases.
  These results support prescribed-mapping Geo-FNO as a practical starting point for the variable-gap problem studied here when a suitable geometry mapping is available, while Transolver achieves the highest prediction accuracy with sufficient training data.

articles.agent: アルゴリズム担当エージェント
articles.title_original: Neural Classifiers as Error-Correcting Codes
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.18239v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: A unified framework is proposed that characterizes supervised deep classification as the decoding of error-correcting codes in the Shannon sense. Cross-entropy optimization is shown to align softmax classifiers with maximum-likelihood decoding, where logits map to Hamming distances to class-specific codewords. This correspondence explains the emergence of standard divergence objectives (e.g., Kullback-Leibler, Jeffreys, Bregman) and provides a geometric basis for the stability of decision boundaries. Furthermore, the geometries of Neural Collapse and LeJEPA are identified as optimal constellations for decoding under isotropic noise. Unlike classical Error-Correcting Output Codes, deep networks are shown to learn effective codebooks in the feature space implicitly. This insight is leveraged to derive novel criteria for lossless quantization, improved knowledge distillation, and architectural regularization based on code redundancy. Finally, this perspective is extended to self-supervised encoders, offering a cohesive explanation for the geometry of latent representations in modern neural models.

articles.agent: アルゴリズム担当エージェント
articles.title_original: Asymptotic Margins and Feature Confinement in Conic Classification Heads under Softmax Cross-Entropy
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.18507v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Classification heads built on conic functions give each class a bounded region of the feature space, and such regions are used to reject samples of unseen classes. We ask whether these regions also keep the features bounded when the head is trained with softmax cross-entropy. For a head whose class scores combine a linear term with a Euclidean norm, we first show that the region of each class is bounded by a quadric of revolution, whose eccentricity is the reciprocal of one learned ratio. We then attach to each class an asymptotic margin, which compares the growth of its score with the growth of all the other scores and can be computed by a second-order cone program. The loss of a class has infimum zero exactly when its margin is positive, and it then approaches zero only along diverging features. When the margin is negative, the loss is coercive and its minimizers lie in an explicit ball. Since softmax depends only on the differences between scores, a class with a bounded region can still have a positive margin, so bounded regions do not confine the features. The result extends to other norms, including the polyhedral conic functions. On CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, all 1210 cells of 67 trained conic heads have positive margins, whereas a prototype head keeps nine of its ten cells bounded, as the theory predicts.

articles.agent: アルゴリズム担当エージェント
articles.title_original: SLICES: A Benchmark and Evaluation Framework for Self-Supervised Learning on Sparse ICU Time Series
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.18868v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) results for intensive care unit (ICU) time series are hard to compare when data processing, encoders, and adaptation vary together. We present SLICES, a benchmark and evaluation framework for comparing and extending SSL methods under a shared clinical setup. It fixes 24-hour value and observation-mask inputs, a Transformer encoder, patient-level splits, four endpoints, two adaptation protocols, and five matched seeds across MIMIC-IV, eICU-CRD, and their pooled union. Masked autoencoding (MAE), joint-embedding prediction (JEPA), and contrastive learning provide reference implementations. Among these objectives, MAE leads mean AUPRC in all nine frozen classification comparisons, also under converged probes, and in seven of nine fine-tuning comparisons. Fine-tuned MAE leads hospital mortality at full labels and scores higher than a supervised Transformer of the same architecture at every label fraction, and SSL fine-tuning gives the lowest length-of-stay error. Supervised baselines remain strong elsewhere: GRU-D leads 24-hour mortality and XGBoost leads acute kidney injury in all three regimes. Rankings depend on the adaptation protocol, the comparator set, and whether the probe loss matches the metric. A two-seed MIMIC-IV rerun with the maintained code stays within two across-seed SDs of the reference in all 48 downstream runs. The code repository supports new objectives, shared downstream evaluation, and regeneration of the reference results, so new SSL methods can be compared with these references under the same conditions. Generalization to unseen hospitals is not tested here and is the natural next extension.

articles.title_original: Auditing World-Model Explanations in Retail Forecasting: Faithfulness, Accuracy and Price Response
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.20811v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Forecasting models that read the price and promotion plan explain each forecast as a baseline, what would sell with nothing planned, plus the lift the plan adds, and merchants order stock and plan promotions on that lift. We show that an explanation can pass the checks used to trust it and still be wrong enough to cost money. We define eight checks for any forecaster that states a plan lift, six with a pass rule fixed before any result, and run them on a world model and on LightGBM. In generated store data with known effects, the world model passes the checks of construction, stability, price direction and agreement with sales and with LightGBM, yet when merchants plan into high-demand weeks it states 1.33 to 1.40 times the true lift, and 1.23 to 1.42 times in eight variants of that world; LightGBM overstates it too (1.26, and 1.16 to 1.35). Both still pick the right weeks to promote, but stock ordered to the world model's lift is off by 0.44 to 0.48 of the true lift. The world model's stated response to a lasting regular-price change is 4.7 to 6.5 times the true -0.5, an error in kind that only a measured cause finds. Sanity checks for explanations test whether an explanation depends on the model; a decision needs to know whether it is right about the world, and these results show the first does not give the second. For the final tuned world models of our companion paper on nine data sets, baseline and lift add up under each model's own plan on every window, but a deeper price cut lowers the forecast in 29% to 83% of item-week steps on Dominick's. Across 703 configurations from the settings searches, checks passed were not related to accuracy (Spearman 0.02, 95% interval -0.02 to 0.05). A noisy benchmark of price episodes in Dominick's data is reported as a check of direction only.

articles.title_original: VASR: Vector-Aware Assembly Planning with Equivalent Structures and Repair-Cost Feedback
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.20984v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Furniture assembly planning requires inferring subassembly hierarchies from individual parts and a target illustration. Existing raster-based methods do not explicitly exploit the geometric and structural information in SVG drawings. We introduce VASR, a framework that fuses features from a dedicated SVG encoder with visual representations from a pretrained vision-language model to predict assembly hierarchies. To avoid penalizing valid alternatives to a reference assembly tree, we propose Repair-Aware Hierarchical Policy Optimization (RHPO) with hierarchy-preserving equivalence rewards. RHPO further uses repair-cost feedback to favor decisions with lower downstream correction costs among candidates with comparable equivalence-aware rewards. VASR achieves the highest Equivalent-Hard F1 among the evaluated methods, outperforming GPT6-Astra by 17.69 percentage points on the IKEA-derived test set while maintaining strong performance on an independent furniture dataset.

articles.title_original: Multiply Robust Causal Mediation Analysis with Continuous Treatments
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2105.09254v5 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: In many applications, researchers are interested in the direct and indirect causal effects of a treatment or exposure on an outcome of interest. Mediation analysis offers a rigorous framework for identifying and estimating these causal effects. For binary treatments, efficient estimators for the direct and indirect effects are presented by Tchetgen Tchetgen and Shpitser (2012) based on the influence function of the parameter of interest. These estimators possess desirable properties such as multiple-robustness and asymptotic normality while allowing for slower than root-n rates of convergence for the nuisance parameters. However, in settings involving continuous treatments, these influence function-based estimators are not readily applicable without making strong parametric assumptions. In this work, utilizing a kernel smoothing approach, we propose an estimator suitable for settings with continuous treatments inspired by the influence function-based estimation strategy. Our proposed approach employs cross-fitting, relaxing the smoothness requirements on the nuisance functions and allowing them to be estimated at slower rates than the target parameter. Additionally, similar to influence function-based estimators, our proposed estimator is multiply robust and asymptotically normal, allowing for inference in settings where parametric assumptions may not be justified.
