articles.title_original: Nanorobot queue: Cooperative treatment of cancer based on team member communication and image processing
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2111.11236v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Although nanorobots have been used as clinical prescriptions for work such as gastroscopy, and even photoacoustic tomography technology has been proposed to control nanorobots to deliver drugs at designated delivery points in real time, and there are cases of eliminating "superbacteria" in blood through nanorobots, most technologies are immature, either with low efficiency or low accuracy, Either it can not be mass produced, so the most effective way to treat cancer diseases at this stage is through chemotherapy and radiotherapy. Patients are suffering and can not be cured. Therefore, this paper proposes an ideal model of a treatment method that can completely cure cancer, a cooperative treatment method based on nano robot queue through team member communication and computer vision image classification (target detection).

articles.title_original: High-Dimensional Tail Index Regression
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2403.01318v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Motivated by the empirical observation of power-law distributions in the credits (e.g., ``likes'') of viral posts on social media, we introduce a high-dimensional tail index regression model and propose methods for estimation and inference of its parameters. First, we propose a regularized estimator, establish its consistency, and derive its convergence rate. Second, we construct a debiased version of the regularized estimator to facilitate inference and prove its asymptotic normality. Monte Carlo simulation studies corroborate our theoretical findings. We apply these methods (1) to the text analysis of viral posts on X (formerly Twitter) and (2) to the analysis of abnormally high health expenditures.

articles.title_original: Clustering in pure-attention hardmax transformers and its role in sentiment analysis
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2407.01602v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Transformers are extremely successful machine learning models whose mathematical properties remain poorly understood. Here, we rigorously characterize the behavior of transformers with hardmax self-attention and normalization sublayers as the number of layers tends to infinity. By viewing such transformers as discrete-time dynamical systems describing the evolution of points in a Euclidean space, and thanks to a geometric interpretation of the self-attention mechanism based on hyperplane separation, we show that the transformer inputs asymptotically converge to a clustered equilibrium determined by special points called \textit{leaders}. We then leverage this theoretical understanding to solve sentiment analysis problems from language processing using a fully interpretable transformer model, which effectively captures `context' by clustering meaningless words around leader words carrying the most meaning. Finally, we outline remaining challenges to bridge the gap between the mathematical analysis of transformers and their real-life implementation.

articles.title_original: AI Simulations Grounded in Rich Self-Reports Increase Accuracy and Reduce Distortion
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2411.10109v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: AI simulations of people built from demographic prompts often misjudge individuals and distort sample-level patterns. We test whether rich self-report data reduce these problems. We developed an AI voice interviewer and conducted two-hour interviews following the American Voices Project protocol with 1,052 U.S. adults, who also completed surveys and behavioral experiments. For each participant, we compared simulations prompted with demographic attributes, self-authored personas, survey responses, interview responses, or combined surveys and interviews. We evaluated accuracy on held-out responses, and measured eight statistical distortions at the sample level: biased averages, compressed variance, distorted response distributions, over-correlated items, attitudes collapsing onto one dimension, ideological sorting, amplified experimental effects, and hyper-rationality. On General Social Survey (GSS) items, demographic simulation led to 60.4% accuracy, whereas interview and survey simulation achieved 69.4% and 69.3%, and combining them reached 72.8%, compared with 79.5% for participants' two-week test-retest agreement. Surveys and interviews also improved prediction of personality traits, but not of incentivized economic choices. Combined interview and survey simulation closed a median of 53.5% of the eight distortion gaps between demographic simulation and participant responses. An open-weight model fine-tuned on other participants' self-reports and responses to the target questions achieved 75.2% GSS accuracy and closed a median of 69.3% of the distortion gap. Overall, both frontier and fine-tuned models reduced distortions without erasing them, but neither reduced hyper-rationality in economic games. These findings demonstrate that qualitative and quantitative self-reports can improve person-specific simulations and reduce statistical distortions.

articles.title_original: Scalable Learning from Probability Measures with Mean Measure Quantization
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2502.04907v5 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We consider statistical learning problems in which data are observed as a set of probability measures. Optimal transport (OT) is a popular tool to compare and manipulate such objects, but its computational cost becomes prohibitive when the measures have large support. We study a quantization-based approach in which all input measures are approximated by $K$-point discrete measures sharing a common support. We establish consistency of the resulting quantized measures. We further derive convergence guarantees for several OT-based downstream tasks computed from the quantized measures. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves performance comparable to individual quantization while substantially reducing runtime.

articles.title_original: Quantum Cognition Machine Learning for Forecasting Chromosomal Instability
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2506.03199v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: The accurate prediction of chromosomal instability from the morphology of circulating tumor cells (CTCs) enables real-time detection of CTCs with high metastatic potential in the context of liquid biopsy diagnostics. However, it presents a significant challenge due to the high dimensionality and complexity of single-cell digital pathology data. Here, we introduce the application of Quantum Cognition Machine Learning (QCML), a quantum-inspired computational framework, to estimate morphology-predicted chromosomal instability in CTCs from patients with metastatic breast cancer. QCML leverages quantum mechanical principles to represent data as state vectors in a Hilbert space, enabling context-aware feature modeling, dimensionality reduction, and enhanced generalization without requiring curated feature selection. QCML outperforms conventional machine learning methods when tested on out of sample verification CTCs, achieving higher accuracy in identifying predicted large-scale state transitions (pLST) status from CTC-derived morphology features. These preliminary findings support the application of QCML as a novel machine learning tool with superior performance in high-dimensional, low-sample-size biomedical contexts. QCML enables the simulation of cognition-like learning for the identification of biologically meaningful prediction of chromosomal instability from CTC morphology, offering a novel tool for CTC classification in liquid biopsy.

articles.title_original: Evaluating and Mitigating Skin Color Bias in Skin Lesion Classificatio
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2506.11627v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Skin lesion classifiers may overlook performance disparity because of subtle skin tone variations by treating skin tone as a categorical attribute. This study proposes a method that represents skin tone as a continuous attribute and assigns individual weights to each sample based on its nonlinear relationship with classification performance. Evaluations on two dermatological datasets showed that fairness metrics were sensitive to skin-color categorization. The proposed method also demonstrated more stable fairness improvements than conventional categorical reweighting while generally preserving classification performance.

articles.agent: アルゴリズム担当エージェント
articles.title_original: First-order methods for stochastic and finite-sum convex optimization with deterministic constraints
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2506.20630v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: In this paper, we study a class of stochastic and finite-sum convex optimization problems with deterministic constraints. Existing methods typically aim to find an $\epsilon$-$expected\ feasible\ stochastic\ optimal$ solution, in which both the expected constraint violation and the expected optimality gap are within a prescribed tolerance $\epsilon$. However, in many practical applications, constraints must be nearly satisfied with certainty, rendering such solutions potentially unsuitable due to the risk of substantial violations. To address this issue, we propose stochastic first-order methods for finding an $\epsilon$-$surely\ feasible\ stochastic\ optimal$ ($\epsilon$-SFSO) solution, where the constraint violation is deterministically bounded by $\epsilon$ and the expected optimality gap is at most $\epsilon$. Our methods apply an accelerated stochastic gradient (ASG) scheme or a modified variance-reduced ASG scheme $only\ once$ to a sequence of quadratic penalty subproblems with appropriately chosen penalty parameters. We establish first-order oracle complexity bounds for the proposed methods in computing an $\epsilon$-SFSO solution. Preliminary numerical results are presented to illustrate the performance of the proposed methods.

articles.title_original: Mix-Opt: Mixed Optimization for Memory-Efficient Personalization of Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2507.10029v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Memory-efficient personalization is essential for adapting text-to-image diffusion models while preserving user privacy and operating within the limited computational resources of edge devices. To this end, we propose Mix-Opt, a novel mixed optimization framework that adaptively chooses between backpropagation on low-resolution images (BP-low) and zeroth-order optimization on high-resolution images (ZO-high), guided by the characteristics of the diffusion process. As observed in our experiments, BP-low efficiently adapts the model to target-specific features but suffers from structural distortions due to resolution mismatch. Conversely, ZO-high refines high-resolution details with minimal memory overhead but faces slow convergence when applied without prior adaptation. By complementing both methods, our framework leverages BP-low for effective personalization while using ZO-high to maintain structural consistency, achieving memory-efficient and high-quality fine-tuning. To maximize the efficacy of both BP-low and ZO-high, we introduce a timestep-aware probabilistic function that dynamically selects the appropriate optimization strategy during training. This function mitigates overfitting from BP-low at high timesteps, where structural information is critical, while ensuring that ZO-high is applied more effectively as training progresses. Experimental results across both U-Net- and DiT-based diffusion models demonstrate that Mix-Opt achieves competitive personalization performance while significantly reducing memory consumption. Mix-Opt enables scalable, high-quality personalization without modifying the inference process or increasing inference latency.

articles.agent: アルゴリズム担当エージェント
articles.title_original: QUTCC: Quantile Uncertainty Training and Conformal Calibration for Imaging Inverse Problems
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2507.14760v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: While deep learning offers tremendous promise for scientific and medical imaging, any failures and hallucinations (predictions that do not coincide with reality) are hard to pinpoint and can have serious downstream consequences. Uncertainty estimation techniques, such as conformal prediction, can help by predicting statistically valid error bars for a model's prediction. However, popular conformal prediction methods were not designed for high-dimensional image-valued problems and do not take into account spatial correlations within an image during conformal calibration, resulting in larger-than-necessary uncertainty intervals. We propose a practical simultaneous quantile regression method that enables non-linear, spatially-adaptive scaling during conformal calibration. Our method, QUTCC uses a U-Net architecture with a quantile embedding to learn a full conditional quantile distribution during training, and then leverages this non-linear, learned function for spatially-adaptive conformal calibration. At test time, our method can efficiently estimate uncertainty intervals with pixel-marginal coverage guarantees. In addition, QUTCC can also predict pixel-wise conditional probability density estimates without any built-in distributional assumptions. We evaluate our method on several denoising problems, accelerated magnetic resonance imaging, and quantitative phase microscopy. Our method consistently produces tighter uncertainty intervals than prior conformal methods at the same coverage level, can predict plausible conditional distributions for different tasks, and in some cases, high-uncertainty regions can help us locate hallucinations in a model's prediction.

articles.agent: アルゴリズム担当エージェント
articles.title_original: An open dataset of gas adsorption in deformable metal-organic frameworks for direct air capture
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2508.03162v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Engineering economical and scalable processes for direct air capture (DAC) from humid air relies on atomistic modeling to search and identify promising sorbent materials from a vast chemical space. Machine learning has emerged as a powerful tool for predicting material properties in an efficient yet accurate manner, but these models require large sets of carefully curated training data. We present the Open DAC 2025 (ODAC25) dataset comprising nearly 60 million DFT single-point calculations for CO2, H2O, N2, and O2 adsorption in ~15,000 MOFs. ODAC25 introduces functionalized MOFs, high-energy adsorbate placements, and synthetically generated frameworks to maximize the versatility of models trained on the dataset. ODAC25 improves upon the accuracy of DFT calculations in previous works and applies engineering intuition from recent work regarding the treatment of adsorbate-induced MOF flexibility. We release state-of-the-art machine-learned interatomic potentials trained on ODAC25 and demonstrate their utility via Henry's coefficient predictions. ODAC25 enables MOF screening for DAC at a resolution previously unattainable.

articles.agent: アルゴリズム担当エージェント
articles.title_original: JigSLO: Solving the Resource Puzzle for Efficient Multi-LLM Serving
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2509.06261v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: GPU spatial sharing co-locates instances with complementary demands, such as compute-bound prefill and memory-bound decode, promising cost-efficient multi-LLM serving. Prior systems partition compute and coordinate shared memory capacity, but do not model bandwidth contention among co-located instances of heterogeneous LLMs. This contention makes each instance's latency depend on the memory-access patterns of its co-runners, even when its own resource allocation remains unchanged. Drawing on extensive measurements, we find that the latency impact of bandwidth contention can be captured by a time-shared memory-access model with contended and uncontended periods, so the overall latency can be analytically estimated as a time-weighted average of the latency estimates for these periods. We propose JigSLO, a contention-aware multi-LLM serving system that manages memory resources and schedules each model's prefill and decode phases as separate instances, treating their co-location as a placement decision. Its contention-aware predictor estimates per-instance latency under any co-location from standalone profiles alone. Guided by these predictions, its placement algorithm jointly selects each instance's tensor parallelism, compute share, and batch configuration, pairing complementary memory-access patterns to maximize throughput within each model's latency targets. JigSLO's shared resource manager complements this on the capacity side, sharing weights, pooling KV cache, and transferring it between prefill and decode instances. Across three datasets covering chat, code generation, and long-context summarization, JigSLO outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by $2.3\times$ in SLO attainment and $1.2\times$ in throughput on average, matching their best attainment with half the GPUs on long-context workloads.

articles.agent: アルゴリズム担当エージェント
articles.title_original: SURFing to the Fundamental Limit of Jet Tagging
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2511.15779v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Beyond the practical goal of improving search and measurement sensitivity through better jet tagging algorithms, there is a deeper question: what are their upper performance limits? Generative surrogate models with learned likelihood functions offer a new approach to this problem, provided the surrogate correctly captures the underlying data distribution. In this work, we introduce the SUrrogate ReFerence (SURF) method, a new approach to validating generative models. This framework enables exact Neyman-Pearson tests by training the target model on samples from another tractable surrogate, which is itself trained on real data. We argue that the EPiC-FM generative model is a valid surrogate reference for JetClass jets and apply SURF to show that modern jet taggers may already be operating close to the true statistical limit. By contrast, we find that autoregressive GPT models unphysically exaggerate top vs. QCD separation power encoded in the surrogate reference, implying that they are giving a misleading picture of the fundamental limit.

articles.agent: アルゴリズム担当エージェント
articles.title_original: A physics-constrained neural solver for incompressible flows without labeled data
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2511.18820v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We present a physics-constrained neural solver for incompressible flow that requires neither labeled data nor supervised pretraining. The solver enforces incompressibility and boundary conditions (BCs) to strict tolerances. We attribute the limited Reynolds numbers of existing physics-informed approaches to insufficient enforcement of these constraints, on which conventional finite-difference and finite-volume solvers depend. We therefore formulate incompressible flow as a constrained optimization problem within the physics- and equality-constrained artificial neural network (PECANN) framework: the pressure Poisson residual is minimized subject to the momentum equations, continuity equation, and BCs imposed as equality constraints on the primitive variables, while a conditionally adaptive augmented Lagrangian method enforces each constraint. The pressure Poisson objective proves critical. Across all benchmarks, replacing it with the momentum residual fails to converge to accurate solutions under identical architecture and constraint enforcement, which we attribute to the global elliptic coupling of pressure and velocity that local momentum-residual minimization lacks. For advection-dominated flows, we introduce an adaptive vanishing entropy viscosity that stabilizes training while leaving the converged solution unchanged. The solver predicts lid-driven cavity flow up to Re = 7,500 with centerline velocity profiles matching benchmark data, and is further validated on flow over a backward-facing step at Re = 800, 3D unsteady Beltrami flow, and steady and unsteady flow past a circular cylinder under an inflow-outflow configuration, for which an ablation study identifies admissible outlet BCs for velocity and pressure. From a randomly initialized network and without external perturbations, the solver captures the spontaneous onset of periodic vortex shedding in unsteady cylinder flow.

articles.agent: アルゴリズム担当エージェント
articles.title_original: Toward AI epidemiology: a measurement standardization framework for prospective risk detection
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2512.15783v5 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: This paper proposes a measurement standardization framework that compresses expert-AI interactions into structured, comparable fields for prospective risk detection in deployed AI systems, without access to model internals. This concept paper defines the framework's scope, semantically and statistically, and specifies a protocol for its empirical testing. The population-level claims it is designed to support therefore belong to a staged research program rather than to results claimed here. Measurement standardization underpins three claims. The first is a reliability claim: under bounded conditions, large language models can produce reliable, standardized assessments of the evidential and policy alignment of expert-AI interactions. The second is a governance claim: alignment scores give experts an immediate signal during deployment and give institutions a basis for monitoring alignment patterns across mission types, models, and domains. The third is an outcome validation claim: once measurement standardization is established, aggregate alignment scores could be used to study associations with downstream outcomes in regulated professional settings. This introduces the possibility of an "AI epidemiology", a form of risk detection based on correlated variables instead of mechanistic analysis, inspired by epidemiological reasoning. A minimal application of the protocol to a published expert-AI corpus shows that the judge reproduces its policy and evidential alignment scores across two runs under the specified conditions. Judge reliability at scale remains to be validated in future work. The paper sets out a defined grammar of eight interaction fields, together with a statistical protocol based on paired bootstrap inference, DeLong's test for paired AUCs as a sensitivity check, a pre-specified one-sided non-inferiority margin of 0.05, and Holm-Bonferroni correction.

articles.agent: アルゴリズム担当エージェント
articles.title_original: CORE: Concept-Oriented Reinforcement for Bridging the Definition-Application Gap in Mathematical Reasoning
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2512.18857v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often solve challenging math exercises yet fail to apply the concept right when the problem requires genuine understanding. Popular Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) pipelines reinforce final answers but provide little fine-grained conceptual signal, so models improve at pattern reuse rather than conceptual applications. We introduce CORE (Concept-Oriented REinforcement), an RL training framework that turns explicit concepts into a controllable supervision signal. Starting from a high-quality, low-contamination textbook resource that links verifiable exercises to concise concept descriptions, we run a sanity probe showing LLMs can restate definitions but fail concept-linked quizzes, quantifying the conceptual reasoning gap. CORE then (i) synthesizes concept-aligned quizzes, (ii) injects brief concept snippets during rollouts to elicit concept-primed trajectories, and (iii) reinforces conceptual reasoning via trajectory replacement after group failures, a lightweight forward-KL constraint that aligns unguided with concept-primed policies, or standard GRPO directly on concept-aligned quizzes. Across several models, CORE delivers consistent gains over vanilla and SFT baselines on both in-domain concept-exercise suites and diverse out-of-domain math benchmarks. CORE unifies direct training on concept-aligned quizzes and concept-injected rollouts under outcome regularization. It provides fine-grained conceptual supervision that bridges problem-solving competence and genuine conceptual reasoning, while remaining algorithm- and verifier-agnostic.

articles.agent: アルゴリズム担当エージェント
articles.title_original: On the use of case estimate and transactional payment data in neural networks for individual loss reserving
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2601.05274v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: The use of neural networks trained on individual claims data has become increasingly popular in the actuarial reserving literature. We consider how to best input historical payment data in neural network models. Additionally, case estimates are also available in the format of a time series, and we extend our analysis to assessing their predictive power. In this paper, we compare a feed-forward neural network trained on summarised transactions to a recurrent neural network equipped to analyse a claim's entire payment history and/or case estimate development history. We draw conclusions from training and comparing the performance of the models on multiple, comparable highly complex datasets simulated from SPLICE (Avanzi, Taylor and Wang, 2023). In environments where covariate data is limited, we find evidence that case estimates will improve predictions substantially, but that equipping the neural network with memory only leads to meagre improvements. Although the case estimation process and quality will vary significantly between insurers, we provide a standardised methodology for assessing their value.

articles.agent: アルゴリズム担当エージェント
articles.title_original: A Cherry-Picking Approach to Large Load Shaping for More Effective Carbon Reduction
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2601.17990v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Shaping multi-megawatt flexible loads such as data centers alters generator dispatch on the electric grid, affecting system-wide CO2 emissions and wholesale electricity costs. However, evaluating prevalent load-shaping signals - such as grid-average carbon intensity, locational marginal price, renewable generation, or commercial marginal emission estimates - has remained difficult because full-scale market-clearing models and generator bid data are rarely accessible outside system operators. Here we conduct year-long causal dispatch counterfactuals using a calibrated, nearly 8,900-bus replica of ERCOT's day-ahead Security Constrained Unit Commitment and Security Constrained Economic Dispatch market-clearing process across renewable-rich and fossil-dominated zones. We find that while LMP-based shaping outperforms other static signals in annual grid CO2 reductions, no single signal performs best across all operating conditions. Motivated by these insights, we propose an interpretable daily "cherry-picking" strategy that selects among practicable day-ahead signals using observable grid net demand and nodal minimum LMP, with thresholds learnable directly from historical market data. Cherry-picking achieves 2-3 times greater annual grid CO2 savings than static LMP shaping without increasing wholesale electricity cost relative to flat operation. Extending this framework to coordinated spatial and temporal shifting across two grid nodes increases CO2 reductions by over 70% compared to temporal-only shifting. Finally, because shaping load against region-wide average carbon intensity can backfire and raise physical grid emissions in fossil-heavy zones, our findings highlight the need for Scope 2 carbon-accounting frameworks to incorporate locational, price-aware, and congestion-aware signals.

articles.agent: アルゴリズム担当エージェント
articles.title_original: HyperKKL: Enabling Non-Autonomous State Estimation through Dynamic Weight Conditioning
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2602.22630v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: This paper proposes HyperKKL, a novel learning approach for designing Kazantzis-Kravaris/Luenberger (KKL) observers for non-autonomous nonlinear systems. While KKL observers offer a rigorous theoretical framework by immersing nonlinear dynamics into a stable linear latent space, its practical realization relies on solving Partial Differential Equations (PDE) that are analytically intractable. Current existing learning-based approximations of the KKL observer are mostly designed for autonomous systems, failing to generalize to driven dynamics without expensive retraining or online gradient updates. HyperKKL addresses this by employing a hypernetwork architecture that encodes the exogenous input signal to instantaneously generate the parameters of the KKL observer, effectively learning a family of immersion maps parameterized by the external drive. We rigorously evaluate this approach against a curriculum learning strategy that attempts to generalize from autonomous regimes via training heuristics alone. The novel approach is illustrated on four numerical simulations in benchmark examples including the Duffing, Van der Pol, Lorenz, and R\"ossler systems.

articles.agent: アルゴリズム担当エージェント
articles.title_original: PRUE: A Practical Recipe for Field Boundary Segmentation at Scale
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2603.27101v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large-scale maps of field boundaries are essential for agricultural monitoring tasks. Existing deep learning approaches for satellite-based field mapping are sensitive to illumination, spatial scale, and changes in geographic location. We conduct the first systematic evaluation of segmentation and geospatial foundation models (GFMs) for global field boundary delineation using the Fields of The World (FTW) benchmark. We evaluate 18 models under unified experimental settings, showing that a U-Net semantic segmentation model outperforms instance-based and GFM alternatives on a suite of performance and deployment metrics. We propose a new segmentation approach that combines a U-Net backbone, composite loss functions, and targeted data augmentations to enhance performance and robustness under real-world conditions. Our model achieves a 76% IoU and 47% object-F1 on FTW, an increase of 6% and 9% over the previous baseline. Our approach provides a practical framework for reliable, scalable, and reproducible field boundary delineation across model design, training, and inference. We release all models and model-derived field boundary datasets for five countries.

articles.agent: アルゴリズム担当エージェント
articles.title_original: When VLMs 'Fix' Students: Identifying and Penalizing Over-Correction in the Evaluation of Multi-line Handwritten Math OCR
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2604.22774v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Accurate transcription of handwritten mathematics is crucial for educational AI systems, yet current benchmarks fail to evaluate this capability properly. Most prior studies focus on single-line expressions and rely on lexical metrics such as BLEU, which fail to assess the semantic reasoning across multi-line student solutions. In this paper, we present the first systematic study of multi-line handwritten math Optical Character Recognition (OCR), revealing a critical failure mode of Vision-Language Models (VLMs): over-correction. Instead of faithfully transcribing a student's work, these models often "fix" errors, thereby hiding the very mistakes an educational assessment aims to detect. To address this, we propose PINK (Penalized INK-based score), a semantic evaluation metric that leverages a Large Language Model (LLM) for rubric-based grading and explicitly penalizes over-correction. Our comprehensive evaluation of 15 state-of-the-art VLMs on the FERMAT dataset reveals substantial ranking reversals compared to BLEU: models like GPT-4o are heavily penalized for aggressive over-correction, whereas Gemini 2.5 Flash emerges as the most faithful transcriber. Furthermore, human expert studies show that PINK aligns significantly better with human judgment (55.0% preference over BLEU's 39.5%), providing a more reliable evaluation framework for handwritten math OCR in educational settings. Code is available at https://github.com/9115jin/PINK.

articles.title_original: On Minimal Observation Time for Recovering Latent Hawkes Networks
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2605.08400v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Dynamics of interacting systems in engineering, society, and nature often evolve over latent networks that govern which entities can interact. We study the problem of inferring these networks from event-based observations, which arise naturally in finance, seismology, and neuroscience. While there is substantial algorithmic work addressing this important problem, theoretical results are scarce. In this paper we ask the following fundamental question: what is the minimum time that one must observe the dynamics in order to exactly recover the underlying network, as a function of the number $d$ of interacting entities? For a class of stationary Hawkes processes with sparse, weak interactions, we prove that an observation time of order $\log d$ is sufficient and necessary. For the upper bound we construct a two-stage estimator that uses clipped and binned event data for screening, followed by a least-squares refinement, and apply concentration bounds derived from the Poisson cluster representation. For the lower bound we combine Fano's inequality with Jacod's Girsanov formula for point processes on a suitable subclass of networks.

articles.title_original: Measuring and Decomposing Mode Separation via the Canonical Diffusion
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2605.08777v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Mode separation, namely how sharply a distribution fragments into barrier-separated clusters, is a fundamental geometric property of densities, difficult to quantify in high dimensions. Modes are often the meaningful alternatives in the data, such as the conformations of a molecule or the distinct semantic types among a generative model's outputs. Mode separation is distinct from dispersion, which is what standard label-free tools capture: differential entropy rises with spread regardless of fragmentation, and PCA orders directions by variance regardless of barriers. Mutual information does capture it, but only given the latent component labels, which are usually unavailable. We measure mode separation through a single stochastic process intrinsic to the density, namely the unique reversible diffusion with $f$ as its stationary distribution and a constant scalar diffusion coefficient. From its autocovariance matrix we extract two readouts. The first, SSA (Sum of Squared Autocorrelations), is a scalar barrier-sensitive measure. The second, DA (Dominant Autocorrelation directions), gives linear projections ordered by metastability rather than variance. Under an isotropic-Gaussian null, we derive the limiting spectrum of the empirical autocovariance in closed form, generalizing the Marchenko--Pastur law. Its upper edge gives a noise floor that separates metastable directions from sampling noise. Both readouts use only samples and a score function, scaling to high dimensions through pretrained score-based generative models via Tweedie's identity. We apply our framework to three settings: (i) synthetic Gaussian mixtures, where SSA tracks mutual information; (ii) SDXL text-to-image generations, where SSA and DA capture structure that entropy and PCA miss; and (iii) molecular dynamics of alanine dipeptide, where DA recovers the known slow backbone dihedrals from static samples alone.

articles.title_original: Quantum-to-Quantum Transfer Learning Exhibits Improved Robustness in Low-Data Regimes
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2605.09118v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Transfer learning under limited data is a challenging setting, where models must adapt to new tasks with minimal supervision. Prior work has primarily focused on improving absolute accuracy in transfer learning. However, empirical evidence comparing quantum and classical models in realistic transfer learning settings remains limited, especially in low-data regimes. In this work, we systematically study the robustness of quantum models under reduced training data. We evaluate multiple quantum and classical architectures across diverse transfer tasks and retraining configurations, and quantify robustness using accuracy degradation and relative performance retention (RPR). Our results show that, although classical models often achieve higher peak performance, they exhibit significantly larger degradation when training data is limited. In contrast, quantum models maintain more stable performance across data regimes, indicating improved robustness and data efficiency. These findings provide empirical evidence that quantum models can offer improved robustness in low-resource transfer learning scenarios.

articles.title_original: Sharp feature-learning transitions and Bayes-optimal neural scaling laws in extensive-width networks
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2605.10395v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We study the information-theoretic limits of learning a one-hidden-layer teacher network with hierarchical features from noisy queries, in the context of knowledge transfer to a smaller student model. We work in the high-dimensional regime where the teacher width $k$ scales linearly with the input dimension $d$ -- a setting that captures large-but-finite-width networks and has only recently become analytically tractable. Using a heuristic leave-one-out decoupling argument, validated numerically throughout, we derive asymptotically sharp characterizations of the Bayes-optimal generalization error and individual feature overlaps via a system of closed fixed-point equations. These equations reveal that feature learnability is governed by a sequence of sharp phase transitions: as data grows, teacher features become recoverable sequentially, each through a discontinuous jump in overlap. This sequential acquisition underlies a precise notion of \textit{effective width} $k_c$ -- the number of learnable features at a given data budget $n$ -- which unifies two distinct scaling regimes: a feature-learning regime in which the Bayes-optimal generalization error $\varepsilon^{\rm BO}$ scales as $ n^{1/(2\beta)-1}$, and a refinement regime in which it scales as $n^{-1}$, where $\beta>1/2$ is the exponent of the power-law feature hierarchy. Both laws collapse to the single relation $\varepsilon^{\rm BO}=\Theta(k_c d/n)$. We further show empirically that a student trained with \textsc{Adam} near the effective width $k_c$ achieves these optimal scaling laws (up to a small algorithmic gap), and provide an information-theoretic account of the associated scaling in model size.

articles.title_original: Quantifying Concentration Phenomena of Mean-Field Transformers in the Low-Temperature Regime
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2605.10931v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Transformers with self-attention modules as their core components have become an integral architecture in modern large language and foundation models. In this paper, we study the evolution of tokens in deep encoder-only transformers at inference time which is described in the large-token limit by a mean-field continuity equation. Leveraging ideas from the convergence analysis of interacting multi-particle systems, with particles corresponding to tokens, we prove that the token distribution rapidly concentrates onto the push-forward of the initial distribution under a projection map induced by the key, query, and value matrices, and remains metastable for moderate times. Specifically, we show that the Wasserstein distance of the two distributions scales like $\sqrt{{\log(\beta+1)}/{\beta}}\exp(Ct)+\exp(-ct)$ in terms of the temperature parameter $\beta^{-1}\to 0$ and inference time $t\geq 0$. For the proof, we establish Lyapunov-type estimates for the zero-temperature equation, identify its limit as $t\to\infty$, and employ a stability estimate in Wasserstein space together with a quantitative Laplace principle to couple the two equations. Our result implies that for time scales of order $\log\beta$, which correspond to the early-phase behavior most relevant for practical finite-depth models, the token distribution concentrates at the identified limiting distribution. Numerical experiments confirm this and, beyond that, complement our theory by showing that for finite $\beta$ and large $t$ the dynamics enter a different terminal phase, dominated by the spectrum of the value matrix.

articles.title_original: Kernel-based guarantees for nonlinear parametric models in Bayesian optimization
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2605.13160v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Modern Bayesian optimization and adaptive sampling methods increasingly rely on nonlinear parametric models, such as neural networks, yet theoretical guarantees for such models under adaptive data collection remain limited. Existing analyses largely focus on Gaussian processes, kernel machines, linear models, or linearized neural approximations, leaving a gap between theory and the nonlinear models used in practice. We develop a kernel-based framework for analyzing regularized parametric models trained on adaptively collected data. Our approach uses kernels over the parameter space to induce reproducing kernel Hilbert space structures over the corresponding model class, yielding confidence bounds for models trained with a broad class of regularized losses. We show how these bounds can establish convergence guarantees for approximate Thompson sampling and provide a foundation for analyzing broader likelihood-free Bayesian optimization methods. These results provide a unified route to analyzing nonlinear models in Bayesian optimization and related adaptive optimization settings.

articles.title_original: CardioLoom: A Report-Guided Electrocardiogram Foundation Model for Cross-Domain Cardiovascular Phenotyping
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2605.25446v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Routine electrocardiogram (ECG) reports offer scalable supervision for cardiovascular representation learning. In this retrospective study, we pretrained CardioLoom, a report-guided ECG foundation model, on 2,781,289 ECG-report pairs from 1,298,359 patients. Downstream development used a separate cohort of 721,317 ECGs from 233,798 patients. Evaluation covered 89 targets, with external testing in nine cohorts. Across 45 internal ECG diagnoses, macro area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) was 0.624 versus 0.615 for DeepECG-SSL. Across 203 external ECG evaluations, corresponding means were 0.425 and 0.424. Using labels from 10% of training patients, CardioLoom achieved macro-AUPRC 0.559, exceeding supervised training with all labels (0.549). For heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, AUPRCs were 0.690, 0.641 and 0.677 in Zhongshan, Shiyuan and BIDMC. Cardiac amyloidosis screening yielded 4.5% positive predictive value using a threshold targeting 99% specificity in validation. Report-guided pretraining supported label-efficient ECG diagnosis, with variable transfer across echocardiographic phenotypes.

articles.title_original: Batched Stochastic Linear Bandits with 1-Bit Communication Constraints
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2605.30976v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We study stochastic linear bandits under a natural combination of batching and communication constraints: the time horizon is partitioned into batches of equal size $B$, and during each batch the learner sends $B$ requested arm pulls to an agent, who then observes the corresponding $B$ rewards and responds with a single bit of feedback to the learner. For each batch, the learner specifies the 1-bit quantization rule the agent uses, which may depend on all previously received bits but not on any past rewards directly. This setting addresses a significant yet unexplored ``middle ground'' between previous models having per-round quantization only or total bit budgets only. We establish a minimax lower bound showing that $\Omega(B\min\{d,\log\lvert \mathcal{A} \rvert\})$ regret is unavoidable due to the 1-bit communication bottleneck, even in the absence of noise. Combined with standard statistical limits, this yields a general lower bound of $\widetilde{\Omega}(B\min\{d,\log\lvert \mathcal{A} \rvert\} + \sqrt{dT \min\{d,\log\lvert \mathcal{A} \rvert\}})$. We develop two phased-elimination algorithms based on $G$-optimal designs and 1-bit mean estimation. The first achieves $\widetilde{O}(dB + d\sqrt{T})$ regret, matching the lower bound up to logarithmic factors when $\lvert \mathcal{A} \rvert = \exp(\Omega(d))$, and the second incorporates a safe-arm identification and warm-start procedure to obtain $\widetilde{O}(B\log\lvert \mathcal{A} \rvert + d^{3/2}\sqrt{B} + \sqrt{dT\log\lvert \mathcal{A} \rvert})$ regret, which is near-optimal in broad scaling regimes of $(\lvert \mathcal{A} \rvert, B, d, T)$. Together, our results demonstrate that a single bit of feedback per batch suffices to nearly match the minimax regret of unconstrained linear bandits in broad scaling regimes, even for batch sizes as large as $\Theta(\sqrt{T})$.

articles.title_original: Bidirectional Random Projections
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2606.10377v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: This paper analyzes bidirectional random projections for ordinary least squares (OLS) regression under the fixed design setting. Let $(X, Y) \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times p}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}$ be a sample and $W \in \mathbb{R}^{n_1\times n}$, $R \in \mathbb{R}^{p\times p_1}$ be two random projections. We develop an expected excess loss bound for the OLS estimator built on $(WXR, WY)$, extending an established bound for the OLS estimator built on $(XR, Y)$. Our analysis shows that our bound is larger and the gap between the two bounds decays at a rate of approximately $O(1/n_1)$. These findings are confirmed by numerical results.

articles.title_original: Latent Goal Prediction from Language for Model-Based Planning
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2606.20627v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) enable agents to plan in latent space by imagining the outcomes of candidate actions, yet task specification remains a bottleneck. Visual targets provide precise local gradients but poor distant guidance, while language is flexible yet limited by noisy cross-modal alignment or dependence on distinct large generative models. We introduce LAGO (Latent Goal Prediction from Language), a hierarchical world model in which a single predictor both forecasts action-conditioned dynamics and grounds language instructions as sequences of intermediate latent subgoals, training both modes with a single regression objective over a shared latent space. At each planning step, LAGO predicts a sequence of latent subgoals from a language instruction and optimizes an action sequence using a soft-minimum alignment cost that rewards subgoal proximity without enforcing a rigid path. Subgoals are repredicted as the agent's state evolves, turning a single long-horizon instruction into a sequence of locally tractable objectives. Across environments spanning navigation and manipulation, LAGO outperforms flat and hierarchical image-goal planners, with the largest gains on long-horizon navigation with curved, hazard-constrained paths, where it more than doubles the success rate of a goal-conditioned behavior cloning policy trained on the same demonstrations. Grounding language in the world model's own latent space also outperforms vision-language reward models, including one that plans with ground-truth dynamics.

articles.title_original: Statistical Adversaries: Natural Backdoor-like Adversarial Features in Clean Vision Datasets
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2607.05516v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Model-specific adversarial attacks have been extensively studied. We study a different failure mode: naturally occurring statistical signals in vision data that can behave as backdoor-like triggers without being maliciously inserted. We call these signals statistical adversaries. We analyse ImageNet to find patterns that are strongly linked to certain labels. We then use statistical controls to remove random correlations from our candidate signals. Finally, we demonstrate that these signals directly and predictably alter model predictions. These statistical adversaries are more targeted than generic corruptions and transfer across different model architectures. This suggests that some vulnerabilities are driven by dataset structure and distribution rather than a single model's idiosyncrasies. We conclude that ordinary datasets can contain exploitable adversarial surfaces even in the absence of poisoning, and suggest that dataset audits should treat spurious structure not only as a source of bias or interpretability failure, but also as a latent attack surface for vision models.

articles.title_original: Adapting Generalist Vehicle Models for High-Speed MPC Across Terrains
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2607.13319v5 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: High-speed off-road autonomy requires precise closed-loop control for a target vehicle while remaining robust across changing terrains. Recent forward kinodynamic (FKD) prediction foundation models suggest a promising path, starting from a generalist model and specializing it to the target platform. However, effective specialization remains challenging, as it often requires substantial real-world data, and models adapted to one setting can still overfit to specific terrains or driving regimes. We present OptCar (Optimized Car), a recipe for bridging the gap from generalist to specialist FKD models that preserves cross-terrain generalization while optimizing performance for a specific vehicle. OptCar introduces a transformer FKD architecture that uses FiLM to condition multi-step predictions on a single dynamics context token summarizing recent state-action history. It then specializes the generalist model using limited real-world data and targeted synthetic rollouts from environment-specific system identification. In closed-loop model predictive control (MPC) experiments across three terrains and an out-of-distribution cart-pulling task, the largest gains appear at 6 m/s, the highest speed evaluated and the regime in which slip dominates tracking error. On vegetation + dirt, the most slip-diverse terrain, OptCar reduces 6 m/s trajectory tracking error by roughly 55% relative to AnyCar fine-tuned on real data alone, and remains the most accurate even when an unseen cart payload changes the dynamics. With 5 minutes of real data per terrain, OptCar is competitive on road with a specialist trained on 30 minutes of road data and outperforms it when the terrain changes. Project Page : https://amrl.cs.utexas.edu/optcar/

articles.title_original: Test-Time Coverage: Test-Conditioned Data Curation for Deployment-Aware Learning
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2607.22697v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Deployed AI systems are often trained from broad candidate data pools, necessitating data curation towards the deployment test distribution. However, standard data curation methods score training-side criteria rather than directly optimizing deployment match. We introduce TTCov (Test-Time Coverage), a data-level test-conditioned curation method that uses test-side information before training instead of updating model weights at inference. TTCov decomposes deployment-conditioned curation into coverage and distribution. To represent coverage, it builds a task Atlas, a collection of LLM-based atomic propositions (APs) describing deployment-relevant concepts, seeded from open task knowledge and expanded with unmatched APs extracted from unlabeled deployment samples. To represent distribution, it instantiates the matched deployment APs with their frequencies, yielding a Knowledge Atlas (K-Atlas) that operationalizes the deployment distribution as a curation target. TTCov then selects a budgeted training set whose deployment APs distribution approximates this target. We apply TTCov towards autonomous driving (AD), keeping adaptation off the inference path while selecting data with greater deployment-relevant coverage, closer K-Atlas matching, and stronger downstream end-to-end driving performance than data-curation baselines, including seamless adaptability to novel domains via city-to-city expansion. Code available at https://github.com/NVlabs/TTCov.

articles.title_original: MAGIC-SSCIL: Manifold Anchoring and Geometric Incremental Calibration for Semi-Supervised Class Incremental Learning
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2608.07586v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Exemplar-free semi-supervised class-incremental learning (SSCIL) asks a model to learn new classes from a few labeled and many unlabeled images without storing past data. A common recipe replays old classes from stored Gaussian statistics and pseudo-labels unlabeled data with a confidence threshold. With one or two labels per class, however, the model's confidence is a poor guide to which pseudo-labels are right, so the statistics that replay depends on rest on few or noisy samples. We propose MAGIC (Manifold Anchoring and Geometric Incremental Calibration), which propagates labels over a k-nearest-neighbor graph of frozen features and uses the propagated confidences as weights in the unlabeled loss and, through Soft-Weighted Geometry Calibration (SWGC), in the class statistics from which phantom features replay old classes. With a frozen ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100, CUB-200, and ImageNet-R at 1%, 5%, and 10% labels, we compare MAGIC with nine supervised class-incremental methods equipped with FixMatch and two native SSCIL methods. MAGIC gains from unlabeled data in all nine settings, most at 1%, and leads on fine-grained CUB-200 at every ratio; at 1% it is level with the best on ImageNet-R and 2.2 points behind the native SSCIL method TACLE on CIFAR-100. Experiments inside MAGIC show that most of this gain flows through the weighted statistics, not the loss, that at 1% labels graph pseudo-labels are more accurate than the model's own at equal coverage, and that a fixed threshold of 0.95 removes most of the gain. At higher ratios, baselines that adapt the backbone or model full covariances overtake MAGIC on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-R.

articles.title_original: Probing and steering biology across Boltz-1s trunk-diffusion boundary
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2608.11475v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: AlphaFold3-class structure predictors pair a representational trunk, which processes sequence and context, with a diffusion module, which generates atomic coordinates. How biological information changes as it crosses this architectural boundary remains poorly understood. We analyze per-residue activations from the Pairformer trunk and diffusion module of Boltz-1 using linear probes, sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and causal interventions. From the trunk, both geometry (secondary structure, disorder) and sequence chemistry (amino-acid identity, signal peptides, disulfide-bond annotations) are linearly decodable. In the diffusion module, the two diverge. Secondary structure remains equally decodable, whereas sequence chemistry becomes much less linearly accessible. We then test whether decodable directions can steer the model by editing the trunk's single representation. Helix and coil directions change predicted structure dose-dependently, but a beta-strand direction that is highly predictive on the same proteins (held-out F1 =0.78) produces no measurable increase in strand content at any of the steered layers. Removing helix or coil directions does not remove that structure. Linear decodability therefore did not imply causal influence at the sites we tested. The same probes also score markedly lower against SwissProt annotations than against DSSP labels, because unannotated residues that the model gets right are charged as false positives; such scores are therefore lower bounds. Finally, supervised probes outscore single SAE features wherever a label already exists.

articles.title_original: Semantic Prism: Generative Segmentation with an Explicit Semantic-Image Interface
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2608.11537v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Conditional image generators can render segmentation maps as semantic RGB images, but color drift and boundary mixing can undermine direct decoding. We present Semantic Prism, a framework that combines an explicit semantic-image interface with hierarchical refinement for road-scene segmentation. A generator adapted from a diffusion-distilled backbone produces a semantic RGB image with a single denoising update per crop. Distances to a fixed class-color codebook define interface logits and pixelwise class probabilities. Hierarchical Generator Evidence Alignment (HGEA) combines spatially aligned multilevel features from the VAE encoder of the generator with the input image, generated semantic image, and interface probabilities to predict additive corrections to these logits. Contextual Interface Hierarchy Disagreement (C-IHD) combines pointwise uncertainty, local context, and interface-refinement disagreement in a fixed score for ranking pixel errors, without an auxiliary predictor or an additional network pass. On the 500-image Cityscapes validation set, Semantic Prism achieves 72.07% mean mIoU, improving on direct-interface decoding by 11.39 percentage points. Extensive capacity-matched ablations show higher mean mIoU for multilevel refinement than for flat and single-level alternatives. The Cityscapes-trained model transfers to ACDC Dataset, achieving 46.89% mIoU without target-domain adaptation. Beyond Cityscapes, on BDD100K dataset, a separately trained model achieves 62.22% mIoU on its full 1,000-image validation set. Across the 3 evaluated datasets, C-IHD improves pixel-error area under the AUPR over uncertainty derived from maximum softmax probability, with segmentation predictions held fixed for each comparison. In particular, on ACDC, AUPR increases from 0.6580 to 0.7557, demonstrating that Semantic Prism presents more effective error ranking under adverse-condition domain shift.

articles.title_original: On the Feasibility of Image-Based Representations for Air Traffic Complexity Estimation
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2608.11810v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Air traffic controllers perceive traffic complexity through the radar display, suggesting that a computer vision model operating on the same imagery may provide a natural architecture for modeling controller-perceived complexity; however, whether radar imagery is a viable input format for deep learning vision models remains unclear. Unlike natural images, radar images are extremely sparse and self-similar, consisting primarily of a black background and a few visually identical aircraft blobs, while small changes in aircraft positions can substantially alter sector-level complexity. To test whether a vision model can capture these operationally important differences, we encode each traffic situation as a position image supplemented by five channels representing aircraft state variables, including heading, speed, and altitude, and train a Vision Transformer (ViT) to regress four intrinsic complexity components derived from pairwise geometric relations among aircraft. The model achieves $R^2 > 0.96$ for all four components on test data, and a one-aircraft removal perturbation study shows that the change in the model's estimate is proportional to how much the removed aircraft contributed to sector complexity, rather than the same for every removal. These results demonstrate that, despite its atypical visual characteristics, the proposed image-based representation is a viable input format for air traffic complexity modeling.

articles.agent: アルゴリズム担当エージェント
articles.title_original: One Frozen Simulator Is Not Enough: Simulator Collapse in Multi-Agent RL
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2608.12253v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) for human-AI interaction usually trains the agent against a single large language model (LLM) that simulates the user. We show that agents trained this way can systematically fail to generalize, and we trace the failure to simulator collapse: the simulator LLM is mode-collapsed, and a policy trained against it learns narrow strategies that exploit the simulator's mode behavior; these strategies transfer poorly to unseen simulators and to real users. We formalize the collapse and propose two solutions. Verbalized Sampling, applied at inference time, samples each simulator reply from a verbalized response distribution. Co-Training, applied during training similar to self-play, co-evolves the simulator as the policy, so the policy cannot exploit the mode behavior. A population variant samples the simulator for each rollout from a pool of recent checkpoints. We validate both solutions on three benchmarks: Persuasion for Good, tau^2-bench, and CooperBench. Verbalized Sampling improves held-out success by up to 9% over single-simulator RL, and Co-Training pushes gains further to 14%; the human study shows similar gain on real users. Both solutions also preserve the policy diversity that collapses under single-simulator RL. Overall, our findings on simulator collapse point to diverse simulators as a requirement for RL agents that serve real users. We release SCOPE, an open-source framework for Population Co-Training in multi-agent RL.

articles.title_original: Evaluation Resolution Confounds Learning-Rule Comparisons in Model-Brain RSA of Early Visual Cortex
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2608.12408v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Revision note: see Comments. Studies of biologically plausible learning rules (feedback alignment, predictive coding, STDP) train small networks on $32\times32$ images and compare them with brain responses to naturalistic stimuli presented at much higher resolution. We find that a common result in this setting, that untrained or locally trained networks rival or beat backpropagation at early visual cortex, depends on the resolution at which networks are evaluated. In representational similarity analysis (RSA) against human V1, the gap between an untrained and a backprop-trained network grows monotonically from $-0.001$ (95% CI $[-0.011, 0.009]$) at the 32 px training resolution to $+0.030$ $[0.018, 0.042]$ at 224 px (six resolutions, 5 seeds; per-subject RSA on cross-run stimulus pairs). The growth reproduces for three further learning rules, directionally in single-seed macaque electrophysiology, along training, and for an ImageNet ResNet-50 and a Swin-Tiny transformer, which also align best at low resolution although trained at 224 px. Gabor and pixel structure, the normalization state of the untrained baseline, and a global brightness statistic do not account for it. Against a criterion fixed before the analysis, limiting image content to 32 px while the input still grows does not shrink the V1 gap ($+0.035$ $[0.023, 0.046]$ vs. $+0.030$ at 224 px; ratio 1.14 $[1.03, 1.34]$): it arises once the input exceeds the training resolution, through a decline of backprop. A single luminance value per image reaches rho= 0.054 against V1, matching the untrained network (0.053), which bounds what RSA on globally pooled features can resolve at V1 in this dataset. The one learning effect that holds across resolution is backprop above untrained at LOC. Comparisons of learning rules or architectures at early visual cortex need to control, and report, the evaluation resolution.

articles.agent: アルゴリズム担当エージェント
articles.title_original: Why ML-based cough models do not generalize: a systematic cross-dataset evaluation for tuberculosis screening
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2608.25846v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Cough acoustics are promising for non-invasive tuberculosis (TB) screening, yet whether machine learning (ML) models capture disease-related acoustics or artifacts of data collection remains unresolved. We evaluated the cross-dataset generalizability of classical ML and deep learning (DL) cough-based TB classifiers across three independent datasets. Despite moderate within-dataset performance (ROC-AUC up to $0.76 \pm 0.06$), both pipelines fail to generalize, with external performance frequently below 0.6, indicating a possible limitation of the data. We further observed that audio representations are organized by recording device and dataset rather than TB status, predicted TB probability tracks country-level prevalence in CODA, and device mismatch degrades transfer while device-diverse training improves it. Additionally, a clinical-variable baseline generalizes more consistently (ROC-AUC $0.65-0.71$), indicating acquisition-specific variability in acoustics is a stronger driver of poor generalizability. High within-dataset performance is not enough. External validation is essential before cough-based TB models are clinically ready.

articles.agent: アルゴリズム担当エージェント
articles.title_original: Representation Learning with Quantum Signal Processing
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2608.28828v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Representation learning begins when training changes the features that define similarity between data. A frozen-kernel model only reweights a fixed geometry. We establish quantum signal processing (QSP) as a solvable quantum model of the representation-learning regime. At arbitrary depth, we compute the exact mean and variance of its quantum neural tangent kernel, revealing an input-dependent angular geometry whose diagonal remains non-self-averaging even when the underlying unitary approaches Haar randomness. We also prove a sparse-data guarantee for the full nonlinear gradient flow without freezing or ensemble-averaging the kernel: the realized dynamics converges to an integrable scalar flow with a time-dependent kernel closure and explicit convergence times. A finite-depth speed limit holds for every data set and trajectory. At higher data density, numerical results show coupled evolution beyond both the scalar and frozen-kernel descriptions. These results give a controlled theory of learned quantum data geometry with provable training dynamics beyond the frozen limit.

articles.agent: アルゴリズム担当エージェント
articles.title_original: Graph neural networks and the energetic cavity method for combinatorial optimization
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2609.07456v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We study the use of graph neural networks (GNNs) for finding approximate ground states of Ising models. Efficiently finding these ground states is of broad significance because many combinatorial optimization problems can be formulated as an Ising model with the appropriate choice of couplings and fields. Exactly solving these problems is hard but there are many good heuristic methods. A lineage of these heuristics build from mean-field approximations: one approach uses the leading eigenvector of an appropriately defined matrix, another is the min-sum algorithm, also known as the energetic cavity method. Without modification, GNNs perform worse than both of these methods. We consider small modifications to the GNN to incorporate these heuristics and find that this considerably improves performance. While the modified approach is much stronger than other deep learning approaches, we still find that simulated annealing is generally as good for the same computational cost.

articles.title_original: Generative sequence modeling for infinite memory processes via predictive states
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2609.38524v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We consider estimating the one-step-ahead conditional distribution of a multivariate stochastic process. Many existing approaches rely on structural assumptions such as finite-range memory, sparsity, or additivity, which can be poorly suited to processes with long-range nonlinear interactions. However, without such structural assumptions, nonparametric estimation is known to be challenging due to the curse of dimensionality. To address this challenge, we introduce a new estimator based on the idea of learning representations of the \emph{predictive states} of a stochastic process. We theoretically analyze several aspects of this problem. As a bonus, we establish convergence rate guarantees for an instantiation of our method based on deep neural network estimators. Our results suggest that faster convergence rates are achievable when the predictive state space is lower-dimensional. That is, when the past history can be compressed into a lower-dimensional statistic that is sufficient for predicting the future. We implement our method in PyTorch and evaluate its performance on synthetic data and real \emph{C. elegans} data.

articles.title_original: Natural Code Transformation Confuses Agents in Vulnerability Analysis
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.14350v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Having demonstrated a strong potential for automating vulnerability discovery, AI agents can also be used to attack software systems at scale. Today's software systems need mechanisms to level the playing field by slowing down potential attacks, giving them time to patch vulnerabilities and strengthen software. Along this line, our study of agent trajectories in vulnerability analysis shows a surprising finding: agents produce dramatically different results across real-world code commits that carry the same functionality and the same vulnerability. This phenomenon appears consistently in multiple code domains and vulnerability categories.
  It motivates us to study natural and functionality-preserving code transformations derived from real-world software development, and their potential as a defense against attacker agents. We build a corpus of natural transformations by mining recurring development patterns from real-world code commits, and apply them to evaluate impact on agentic vulnerability analysis. Our results show that even a single form of transformation can effectively "confuse" frontier agents, e.g., Claude Mythos 5.2 with Claude Code, reducing successes in vulnerability discovery. We also study different agent failures, whether transformations can be composed to provide stronger protection, and adaptive attackers who seek to reverse them. Overall, our study of natural code transformation significantly expands the research space of using code transformations to defend against malicious agents.

articles.title_original: SarcasTraps: Effect of Sarcasm on Turkish Hate Speech Detection
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.16957v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Standard hate speech detection datasets often emphasize explicit harmful language, but directed harm can also be expressed indirectly, without clearly hateful wording. Sarcasm is one such form of indirect expression, as it can convey harmful intent through mock praise, exaggeration, humor, or apparent politeness. In this paper, we introduce SarcasTraps, a targeted external test set for analyzing the effect of sarcasm on Turkish hate speech detection. SarcasTraps contains 479 entries annotated along two dimensions: hate speech and sarcasm. We train classifiers using BERTurk and XLM-RoBERTa on two existing Turkish hate speech datasets and evaluate them on SarcasTraps, using it strictly as an external test set. We also evaluate GPT-4.1 and Llama-3.3-70B in a zero-shot setting on SarcasTraps. Results show that sarcasm substantially affects hate speech detection. Fine-tuned encoder models lose recall on sarcastic hate, while zero-shot LLMs maintain higher recall but suffer substantial precision drops on sarcastic examples. These findings show that both fine-tuned hate speech detectors and zero-shot LLMs struggle when sarcasm is involved, and SarcasTraps provides quantitative evidence of this challenge through a targeted Turkish test set. Due to the presence of sensitive and hateful language, SarcasTraps will be shared upon request for academic research purposes. Warning: This paper has examples from the dataset which contains offensive and hateful content towards groups of people.

articles.title_original: MemT-1.0: Towards Memory-Native Evolution
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.26825v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Memory-native evolution requires making memory an intrinsic capability of foundation models, enabling them to continuously accumulate and utilize information. To this end, we introduce MemT-1.0, a new architecture of memory foundation models that internalize memory as part of model computation. Building on Metis, MemT-1.0 employs Gated DeltaNet-2 with a stable token-level memory update mechanism within each turn. We further introduce Mixture-of-Storage to scale native memory capacity. Following a deliberate backbone preparation, we develop a two-stage training pipeline consisting of continued pre-training and post-training, supported by 34B tokens of training data and efficient training and inference infrastructure. We release a model family comprising MemT-1.0-Nano, MemT-1.0-Flash, and MemT-1.0-Pro, and conduct a comprehensive evaluation of memory and general capabilities. The results show that they outperform the parametric memory baselines on average and remain competitive with retrieval-augmented methods, while largely preserving general capabilities. At a history length of 128K tokens, MemT-1.0-Nano achieves approximately $1.86\times$ end-to-end inference speedup and a $66\times$ reduction in persistent storage relative to full context KV cache. By internalizing retrieved procedural experience, MemT-1.0 improves task success on agentic tasks, providing a practical step toward memory-native evolution.

articles.title_original: Fixed Sets and the Hardness of Computing Correlated Equilibria
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.28141v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We show that computing an approximate correlated equilibrium of a polytope game is PPAD-complete, and thus polynomial-time equivalent to finding a Nash equilibrium. This challenges the conventional view in game theory that correlated equilibria are more tractable objects than Nash equilibria. From a conceptual standpoint, we connect correlated equilibria to a natural generalization of fixed points, which we call fixed sets. A fixed set of a continuous function $f$ is a nonempty finite set $S$ such that $S \subseteq \operatorname{conv} f(S)$. Our main technical contribution is to prove that computing a fixed set is PPAD-hard even at inverse polynomial precision.

articles.title_original: Not All Mislabels Are Equal: Efficient Task-Aware Auditing with Confidence Sequences
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.33262v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We study efficient, adaptive auditing of categorical labels in a fixed dataset, motivated by biodiversity credit programs in which expert verification of species records is costly and downstream scores (e.g., payment) are more sensitive to errors on certain labels than on others. Our proposed ATLAS framework couples anytime-valid inference with a task-aware adaptive auditing policy. Representing label corrections through a confusion matrix, we prioritize which data points to inspect next based on both label uncertainty and the influence of potential label corrections on the downstream score function. In our main case study on Kenyan biodiversity data, task-aware auditing reduces the expert review needed to estimate both the mislabel rate and the nonlinear biodiversity score while maintaining anytime-valid guarantees. We also evaluate ATLAS on public datasets for image classification and named-entity recognition. Across our experiments with linear and nonlinear scores, ATLAS generally reaches the same precision as competing anytime-valid methods with substantially fewer audits. When distribution-free guarantees are prohibitively costly, we develop a model-based Bayesian alternative that can further reduce the number of audits by relying on modeling assumptions. Our biodiversity case study highlights a gap between statistical validity and practical feasibility: generic methods such as Serfling's bound and existing confidence-sequence procedures are rigorous but can require prohibitively many expert reviews in practice. Together, these results show task-aware auditing can significantly reduce the number of expert audits needed while providing finite-sample, anytime-valid guarantees

articles.title_original: Formalizing the Intrinsic Dimension of Objective Landscapes by a Generalized Notion of Co-dimension
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.39674v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: In this work, we formalize the concept of intrinsic dimension of objective landscapes introduced in Li et al. (2018), which measures the structural complexity of learning problems by training along randomly generated subspaces. We define the intrinsic dimension of a set $\Theta\subset\mathbb{R}^p$ as the minimal dimension $d_{\mathrm{int}}(\Theta)$ such that a random plane of dimension $d_{\mathrm{int}}(\Theta)$ in $\mathbb{R}^p$ intersects $\Theta$ with probability one. We show that it is a generalized notion of co-dimension that depends on the global geometry of $\Theta$. We study mathematical properties of the intrinsic dimension and develop techniques to estimate the intrinsic dimension of sets $\Theta$ that arise in learning problems. More specifically, we derive upper and/or lower bounds where $\Theta$ is the set of optimal parameters in student-teacher settings with shallow and deep ReLU networks, including finite and infinite sample cases, and with and without regularization. We discuss how our theory leads to novel types of generalization bounds, thereby showing that the intrinsic dimension is a measure of learning complexity. Our results connect techniques from seemingly different areas of machine learning research such as classification of symmetries of ReLU networks and stochastic geometry.
